utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mueller, you want to address the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Your Honours, on behalf of my client, I would like to make a statement. My client asks you to lift the order of non-disclosure in this case. He wants to go public, and he's ready to give you the explanations and reasons for that, if you'd like to hear this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness -- if you want to say something briefly about it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: You want me or the witness to tell this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whichever is more convenient. Mr. Mueller, since you're already addressing us, perhaps you'd like to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note there is some difficulty in following in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to start, Mr. Mueller, we'll see if it's cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. The reasons given by my client are four-fold, Your Honours, and this also refers -- this also gives a reason as to why the client has made this decision just now and not on an earlier stage of this trial. The first reason my client gives is this: Within the last weeks, Mr. Milosevic has accused him and was laying blame on him, and this was mostly in closed session. He thinks that the public has an interest and a right to be kept up-to-date about his arguments which were in response of the arguments of Mr. Milosevic. The second reason is that he says, "During my testifying, the press, the media, has meddled my identity by more or less direct references. This spiralled up so far that my photo," personal information about him such as his bio, his full name and his name as C-061 was published in the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Apparently there is some continuing problem with the interpretation. Yes. Let's continue. There is a power system failure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I gather the accused can follow the transcript. Apologies to the amicus. We will not start the evidence, but let us finish this explanation while we can. We're awaiting the technician. Yes, Mr. Mueller.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This went so far that the public in Belgrade, at least in Belgrade, and the media in the meantime knows about his full name and his identity. The third point is the following, Your Honours: My client says that he spoke to his family about this issue, and this was a very long-lasting process within the last weeks, and the family was scared about the release of his identity, and his family has endured a lot of fear in the last time. So as we may know from his statement, and I shouldn't repeat that, perhaps, there were threats to his life. These people is still in a certain way, that's what he believes, threatening his family now. And the discussion on this subject underwent a long, long process within the family and finally a decision was made by yesterday evening that the family agreed when he goes public. And the fourth and very important issue for the client is the following: The way to go public -- the decision to go public, in his view, is a very important contribution to reconciliation of the people in the former Yugoslavia by hearing his opinion and by hearing that what he says is the truth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the witness if one of the factors given by counsel for his decision to go public relates to threats to his family, which apparently are still continuing. I don't understand in that context, then, against that background, how going public would assist. Or is it that the last factor, the reconciliation, which would be encouraged and facilitated, is the predominant factor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I expect that the Tribunal, outside this courtroom, will continue its protective measures to assist my family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. The application will be granted. The measures will be lifted. Mr. Babic, your application to have your protective measures made in relation to you having been granted, you will be referred to by your name. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I understood you to say that I have two hours, 15 minutes left, is that right, for today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and it's now 9.15, nearly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We will resume where we left off. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we left off talking about Kijevo. You explained that this young man who was killed, Pecer Vaso was his name, took part in some sort of shooting between a group on the Serb side and those others, concentrated "orderlies" or "Redarstvenici" or members of the Croatian National Guard or whatever they were called, in Kijevo. However, all the facts and all the witnesses from that time say quite the opposite, and that is that there was no shooting whatsoever from the Serb side and that Vaso Pecer was killed while he was tending to his sheep near Kijevo. Do you happen to remember that that was what happened or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about my first piece of information, the first information that reached me, and that was that we received reports, first of all that the late Vaso Pecer at Polaca was killed as an ordinary citizen by the police or, rather, by somebody at Kijevo. After that, I personally attended the public commemoration following the death of that person, and this took place on the 2nd of May, 1991. I later heard a different piece of information, and I also told you about that, and that is that the late Pecer was on the slopes of Mount Kozjak with a group of individuals who were targeting and cross-shooting with Kijevo. And I said here in the courtroom that it was never established how the man was killed. An investigation was conducted into the affair, but as I said, they did not ascertain how he actually died. And that was around the 2nd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in view of the fact that this incident followed the logics of the killing of an innocent young man, a shepherd looking after his sheep, is it true that this incident that was a very serious one and affected everybody's sentiments, because there weren't cases of that kind until then, was the reason why the citizens, after the funeral, after the funeral of this man Vaso Pecer, spontaneously tried to organise an attack on Kijevo and this was thwarted and prevented by the JNA, because of this emotional reaction, and they wanted to stop further bloodshed? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is this: I know that the people were revolted and disturbed and upset, the citizens of Polaca and Knin. And I was there myself. I saw these people who were ready to march on Kijevo, people from Polaca; they were carrying weapons. But this was stopped. We did not grant permission for that, and I don't think the JNA did either. So this was stopped. And this gave rise to a second wave of reaction on the part of the JNA. That is to say, up until that time, the JNA had already been stationed between Polaca and Kijevo, and this incident triggered off the following situation: The Knin Corps stepped up its presence in the area by bringing out more tank units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But is it quite clear that the JNA prevented further bloodshed following that incident, and is it also clear from what you're saying here and now that the JNA played the role of separating the two parties that might have clashed in an armed conflict? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Events of this kind and the events that took place at the Plitvice lakes and in Borovo Selo as well as in Petrik [phoen], and I have described these events, I've talked about them, and the way in which I've described them shows that they were the reason for which the Yugoslav People's Army brought out its units and deployed them along the line between the Serbs, the demarcation line between the Serbs in Krajina and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what we have just observed now is quite contrary to the schematic and diagram that you described at the start of your testimony. We now assert that a shepherd was killed, a young man was killed. After his funeral, there was a general revolt on the part of the populace, and an attempt was made to engage in a new conflict, but this was thwarted and prevented by the JNA who separated the two sides. And you said that there was a programme according to which some people were trying to incite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. You've made various assertions there. Mr. Babic, do you agree with the way that the accused has put the way this incident started? Do you agree with that or not? You should have the opportunity of saying whether you do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree with what he's saying because these incidents were incited on purpose. It was organised by a DB police group, state security group, in order to provoke an armed conflict between the Serbs and Croats or, rather, between the police of the Republic of Croatia on the one side, and later on the Croatian National Guard on the one side, and the Serb forces in Krajina on the other and that this would lead to the displacement of the JNA or, rather, the coming in of the JNA and having its members deployed in the area. So it's not the way Mr. Milosevic has told it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean, then, that these, as you call them, parallel structures organised the killing of Vaso Pecer in order to provoke an incident and in order to have the army positioned in the area? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am claiming that the parallel structures or, rather, the group from Golubic on several occasions shot at Kijevo, causing armed provocation in order to make the MUP of Croatia on the Kijevo side respond and thus became -- and thus became involved in the situation. And I explained to you what I knew about the case of Vaso Pecer, the shepherd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that means that the armed units that were established there by these Croatian paramilitary formations, they were quite innocent, were they? And the person to blame was Vaso Pecer, for having been killed, and he was killed in order to create a reason for an attack to be launched on the innocent members of the Croatian National Guard Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the innocent man Vaso Pecer, I have already stated what I knew about his killing, and I said that the DB, the state security, and police in Krajina, did cause -- did provoke the other side in order to fan the flames of the conflict and have the JNA become involved in the manner that you set out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if we're talking about the facts, then the facts are these: I assume that we would have to be more specific and precise and not to say that provocations were carried out just like that and then that the army intervened afterwards. Is it true that in those days the Croatian MUP carried out raids on the villages and all the other settlements and areas inhabited by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened is the following, and we have the Otisic case as a case in point, what I knew about that at the time, and this was that the MUP of Croatia or, rather, the police station from Sinj, with police units, ransacked the village of Otisic looking for weapons. This instilled fear in the people, and this was - how shall I put it? - a major incident that was caused by the Croatian police, and it caused great unrest among the Serbs in the area, especially the village of Otisic. And that was the reason why I asked you that the JNA should come in to protect the village of Otisic. However, later on I also heard that a group of men from Otisic caused intimidation and placed mines on the power poles - that's my own knowledge - and later on the incident in Otisic broke out and I said that was the reason for which on the 26th of August, 1991 I discussed this matter with you and asked you that the JNA should intervene over there, and you said, "Hasn't that already been solved?" And in fact on that very morning, I heard later on that the JNA and the units under its control had indeed attacked Kijevo and moved towards Otisic from Biletovo [phoen] and towards Mikovo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now blaming the JNA for protecting you and defending you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm just saying what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's not what happened. Why didn't you mention, as you're talking about Otisic - because I have all the facts before me here - that they ransacked and searched the village of Otisic, that they took three Serbs away to the Split prison, and that they killed a local of the village of Cetina. His name was Dusan Gargenta. Wasn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Otisic. I don't know about Gargenta. I don't remember that, how he died or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know about these people who were taken off, and you don't know that that particular man was killed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Otisic. There was great panic and unrest and fear, and I've already talked about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was it the Serbs that caused that once again, this incident, and then they were the casualties in the incident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought at that time that the Croatian police force, for no reason at all, did things like that in Otisic. However, later on I learnt that a group from -- that the group of people from Otisic was not innocent either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these people from Otisic who were arrested and the man who was killed, they themselves are responsible for having been arrested and the man responsible for having got killed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you what I know about those events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it seems that you know something quite different now to what you knew at the time. All right. But is it true in Vrlika they ill-treated the Serbs, that they destroyed and set fire to their houses, and even at that time your father-in-law, Bozo Skrbic, was killed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, several days before the 26th of August, in fact, the Croatian police and the guard that was there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you give me a yes or no answer? You're going into explanations. All I need is yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him answer. You put a number of things, Mr. Milosevic. He must have the chance to answer. And also you're asking about different incidents. Yes, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, according to my information and knowledge, and also the knowledge I had later on as well, the Croatian police or, rather, the MUP of Croatia in Vrlika and the Croatian guard corps, a unit of the guard corps that was in Vrlika at the time, blocked all exits towards Civljani. That means towards the Knin municipality. And the population, the inhabitants were not able to cross that line. Around the village of Kosori and Civljani was a JNA unit. It was stationed there. This was on the 26th -- no, the 27th of August, 1991. I arrived in Knin in the morning, and later on that same day I arrived in Cgani, and I heard from my mother-in-law that my father-in-law had also been killed in Vrlika by the Croatian police force the previous day, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me now, did your father-in-law provoke the Croatian police in any way or was he to blame for anything so that they killed him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA officers said that -- who were at Cgani and Zukanovici on that day when I myself arrived, which was the 27th of August, they said that by radio communication they had heard conversations between the Croatian police or, rather, the Croatian guard corps. They heard that an order had been issued that all my family should be hanged. My in-laws were there and so was my mother and grandmother. My father-in-law was killed on the occasion, my mother-in-law managed to escape, my house was set fire to, and my mother managed to escape as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you heard the order saying that your family should be hanged. They killed your father-in-law, the rest of your family fled, and so it is the Serb side that is to blame for the incident. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which side do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right, tell me this then, let me put it this way: You mentioned Kijevo and the 1991 fighting. How, then, did you state to the daily paper Politika on the 29th of August, 1991, that no forces from the Republic of Serbia took part in the fighting for the liberation of Kijevo, Vrlika, et cetera, and so on and so forth in that vein, things you said in that particular interview? How is that possible then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember whether I mentioned the Serbian forces, but the fact is that at the battles in Kijevo, it was the JNA that took part, the militia -- the police of Krajina and the local TO defence of the village of Cetina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Tell me, please, is it right that the forces of the 113th Brigade of the National Guards blocked the JNA warehouse and broke into JNA facilities known as Manojlovac, and they mined the road passing through Kijevo and prevented all communication between Knin and Sinj? Is that right? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Manojlovac is on the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about two things.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have mentioned several things. I don't know the exact name of the unit of the National Guard in Drnis in Vrlika. In Kijevo, it was the police of the MUP of Croatia and the unit of the National Guards was in Vrlika and, I also heard, in Drnis. For Manojlovac, I don't know what happened in Manojlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was -- were explosives put along the road to Kijevo and all communication blocked?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, I don't know whether there was a blockade or not. I know that there was communication through Kijevo. It was possible to -- the JNA could move through Kijevo. And even I went by on a couple of occasions in a JNA vehicle through Kijevo with Colonel Djukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So JNA could move freely throughout that period along that route?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, then, that on the 16th of August, the ZNG and MUP from the village of Kijevo, Vrlika, Maovica started attacks on the JNA on all hills and the Kosovska Greda with the aim of destroying and confiscating tanks and APCs? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were conflicts at Civljani, and I think they started on the 26th. I don't know about the 16th, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We noted a moment ago that forces of the 9th JNA corps were deployed along the line Vrlika-Polaca precisely in order to separate the MUP of Croatia and the Serb forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: JNA units were deployed at Polaca, and at Civljani and Kosori, and I expected, after talking to you, that they would also be deployed at Otisic. So they were making a kind of sandwich.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were forming a buffer zone to avoid a conflict. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said how and when the JNA units came. They came under the excuse not to allow a conflict, but the conflict provoked by the DB and the police was the reason that prompted them to take up positions along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So the Serbs manufactured a conflict to have the JNA come out and separate the MUP and ZNGs on the one side and the Serb forces on the other?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were the one who were provoking that conflict through the structures I have referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Babic. And is it true that members of the Croatian MUP opened fire without any cause on facilities and soldiers of the JNA in that buffer zone? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said what I know, that the conflicts between the Croatian citizens, the MUP, and the blockade of the barracks, the Croatian police, and the ZNGs escalated as at the beginning of January 1991 up until August 1991. And in August, they turned into an open war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, then, that after those attacks, it was only then that the forces of the 9th Corps started action primarily to deblock the road?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the following: There was a blockade, and I've already spoken about that in this courtroom. A deceased man from Cetina of whom it was said that he had either died or -- died after being beaten by the Croatian police in Sibenik, and he was buried there. His body was exhumed and they wanted to transport him to Cetina, and that was when the road was blocked. And in that connection, a large meeting, a rally of the citizens was held in front of the 9th Corps. That was the reason for the blockade. So it existed partly only. As for the beginning of the conflict on the 26th of August, I had the following information: First of all, I thought that the blockade of the road had provoked the attack by the JNA. However, I have two other reports about that event. First, on the 25th, in the evening, after I was asked to come and see you in Belgrade, I was told to drop in at Golubici, and over there I saw a group of people from Lapac unloading something into the warehouse where there was a training centre of the DB and police. It seemed to me that I saw the president of the municipality there, and I asked one of the men, "What's going on?" and he said that a mortar platoon from Lapac was going to be deployed in the direction of Kijevo. That is the first report I had about it. Later I heard the following: That a group from Cetina had opened fire first towards Kijevo. So this was a group, whether it was the TO or the police of Krajina or a group of civilians I don't know exactly. Then the fire was returned from Kijevo and then the JNA launched the attack. However, what happened was that the Croatian forces, whether it was the police or ZNG from Jezevici attacked toward Cetina, that the people of Cetina panicked, and they were almost defeated there. But thanks to the rapid intervention of the corps, they managed to defend that route. That is what I heard subsequently about the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You're making a distinction between what you knew then and what you allegedly heard later. What you knew then, you have just repeated, coincides with what I am claiming, and now you're saying that you heard later on that it was different.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I later heard more details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that they too at the time knew that they were going to deblock the road, just as you knew it at the time, and what you're saying now you've made up. Is that right or not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say that the road was deblocked in the way you say it was deblocked, it was done in such a way that -- that all the Croatian population fled before the JNA, that Kijevo was destroyed by artillery, that JNA with tank units and artillery passed through Kijevo towards Vrlika, reached Maovica, Otisic towards Maljkovo, and via Jezevici to the end of the village of Laktaci towards Dabar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That's fine. But let's cover these facts rather quickly. Do you know that no members of the Krajina MUP took part in that operation at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said as much as I knew as to who took part. I know that Martic and Zelenbaba entered Kijevo later on. Whether it was before or after the JNA, I'm not sure. I heard that, but I saw on television that Martic and Milenko Zelenbaba were removing the MUP inscription and they were trampling on it. This was shown on Belgrade television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is quite a different matter. Do you know that Martic, with members of the police, entered Kijevo only after these so-called Croatian policemen - there were 800 of them concentrated there - had fled? And this was a small village. Do you know then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Martic entered Kijevo exactly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know, if you don't know that, since you described how they used tanks and artillery to capture Kijevo and so on, do you know that in that operation of deblocking the road, there were no casualties? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that there were one or two members of the Croatian ZNG buried near Djurdjevici at the entrance to Vrlika. Somebody told me that somebody was buried there. I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So somebody said that one or two people were buried, and I have the information that there were no casualties in the deblocking of Kijevo and that about 60 of them were captured and, immediately after that, released because the purpose was not to kill or arrest anyone but to lift the blockade on the road. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you know you usually say, "I later heard," "Somebody told me," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, I was visiting you in Belgrade and I was not present in Knin or in the area, so it was only the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You keep referring to visiting me in Belgrade very often, but we've seen that when we discussed the Vance Plan in the autumn of 1991, that the next time you saw me was in 1993 as a member of a larger delegation, and in 1994 and 1995. This was only once a year. You seem to give the impression that you were in Belgrade constantly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From October 1990 until September 1991, I met you personally in Belgrade some 25 times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Babic. Those are your claims and assertions. So you are not aware that there were no casualties in Kijevo. You do not know that the 60 men captured were immediately released. You know nothing about that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is what I'm saying correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were captured people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't know. He said that. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he knows that very well, Mr. May, but simply refuses to say anything that suits the Serbian side. But let us move on more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have made -- told us a number of untruths about Drnis. Is it true that Drnis has about an 80 per cent majority Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the HDZ won at the elections and, after asserting its authority, it implemented terror and intimidation and provoking incidents with the Serb population and the JNA? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HDZ won at the elections in Drnis in May 1991. I spoke about the events in the police station in Drnis in August 1990 when Ante Bujas issued an order to a group of policemen over there, who were both Serbs and Croats, to disarm the barricade at Kosovo Klanac and to head toward Drnis. And when the policemen refused to do that, they dispersed. I also said that several local communes in Drnis municipality joined with Knin municipality. I said what I knew about Drnis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that after the formation of the 113th Brigade of the National Guards Corps, attacks on the barracks and warehouses of the JNA started in Sibenik and Split?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what brigade it was in -- correction, Drnis and Sibenik. I don't know the details about the blockade of barracks around Drnis, but there were JNA warehouses there, warehouses, and I do know of the blockade in Sibenik. General Vukovic told me about it and his intention to go and deblock Sibenik via Drnis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about the blockade of barracks, the blockades of the village of Zitnic, the warehouse at Trobunje, the commander of the Motorised Brigade, the radio relay centre, the Manojlovac warehouse? You know nothing about these blockades of barracks and break-ins into warehouses?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were blockades of JNA facilities by the Croatian forces, but I don't know any details about those blockades around Drnis. I know that the garrison in Sibenik was blocked. Exactly where it is and what kind of blockade it was, I don't know. I just know that General Vukovic once asked me whether anyone had a town plan of Sibenik, because he wanted to go and deblock the garrison in Sibenik. And he said in passing that Drnis was like a mole on the female genitals, like a sore on female genitals to him. But I don't know anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were not interested in events then. According to your testimony, you were just a massive observer.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was present at Tepljuh when Orlovic said that the people were disturbed, that there were groups above Tepljuh disturbing them. I went there and saw it. There was no shooting, just incidents. And then an armoured train, Frenki's train, came. There were some disorders there, and then later on, I don't know whether that was the next day or a few days later, I came to Miocic, and General Djukic was already operating there. I reached his armoured combat vehicle. He was issued -- issuing orders to his artillery which was opening fire on Petrovo Polje, and I saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the JNA was a buffer zone along that line, is it true that it prevented conflicts in the village of Tepljuh at the beginning of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly for August, but I do know that it was deployed in front of Miocici and Tepljuh towards Petrovo Polje. This is along the line of villages that had joined Knin. Earlier they were part of Drnis municipality. So between Tepljuh and Croatian villages. And in September there was the event as I have described it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long those small JNA groups were blocked? For example, this centre at Promina was completely blocked, and a transport helicopter which was to bring essentials - food, et cetera - was downed, was shot down by these paramilitary units, and the pilot, Major Brkic, was killed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed there was a blockade but I don't know any details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that negotiations started on a cease-fire and an agreement to that effect was signed and the organised withdrawal of units of the JNA from Sibenik and Sinj?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were talks on several occasions. In August, the JNA, as I said, reached close to Sinj, the village of Maljkovo and close to Drnis, the villages I have mentioned. I know that. And then in September, the beginning of September, the JNA made progress, moved forward towards -- closer to Sinj, the village of Hrvace, and at the end of September the Knin Corps, or Colonel Djukic, captured most of Drnis municipality. He passed through the town of Drnis and established the line at the village of Zitnic. In the area towards Zadar -- I heard this from General Vukovic; he was to deblock Zadar, that is the barracks in Zadar, and this happened at the beginning of October. I do know that General Vukovic, the commander of the 9th Corps, moved its command post to a place near Zemunik and that Zadar was under heavy fire from JNA units and that, in this way, the 9th Corps forced Zadar municipality or, rather, the authorities of that municipality to agree to deblock the barracks and an agreement was signed on deblocking the barracks in Zadar. After that, there were negotiations or incidents, I don't know exactly, around the deblocking of the barracks in Sibenik. So first there was Zadar and then Sibenik. And the garrison from Sinj started pulling out, then from Zadar and then from Sibenik. And this withdrawal went on for months, up until the end of 1991, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So the army intervened regarding two matters only; to deblock its barracks, to pull out its members, its units, and to serve as a buffer zone to prevent conflict between the National Guards Corps and the Serb forces in the area. Isn't that quite clear?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it was deploying within the territory of SAO Krajina but also in areas which were not part of SAO Krajina, such as the town of Drnis, Promina, Miljevci, Kotrelja [phoen], Maljkovo and some other villages around Zadar. Skabrnja, to mention that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any doubt that, at the time, this was all territory of the SFRY and that the army was being deployed in a territory in which it is legally present? And what has that got to do with it if it was not the territory of SAO Krajina? It was deblocking its garrisons in Zadar and Sibenik which were never a part of SAO Krajina, but the army had been there for 50 years, that same army.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the JNA had deblocked the barracks and was moving around SAO Krajina, and in a portion of the area that was not SAO Krajina, which means they took their positions in other areas as well. The SAO Krajina decided to secede from Croatia and to remain within Yugoslavia. It was constituted as a federal territory of the SFRY, according to what -- our convictions. Up until then, the SAO was in fact part of SFRY territory. However, in the parts that I mentioned where the JNA was present and active, this was not SAO Krajina territory. And as for October and November and the subsequent months, it became common knowledge that as of the 8th of October, Croatia declared that the three-month moratorium had expired, after which it could gain independence. And it proclaimed that it was indeed an independent state as of that date. So I'm not here to act as arbiter; I'm just talking about facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the facts. And in that entire operation, in pulling out the army from the facilities that had been deblocked, in pulling out the equipment as well, do you remember the attacks that were made on the railway line between Zagreb and Belgrade and the army trucks, Karlovac and Banja Luka? Another case in point: The Zagreb-Belgrade railway line in the village of Ivankovo when a whole military composition of trains and tracks were attacked by members of the Croatian National Guard Corps, which means that the army was pulling out from the deblocked areas and it was moving out of Croatian territory, in fact. Do you remember that? And the incidents that took place on the Zagreb-Belgrade railway line where a military escort was taken off the train, taken in an unknown direction and military equipment and materiel looted? Do you remember that and everything that attended the blockade and deblocking afterwards and how this situation came to a head and how the feelings escalated vis-a-vis the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described how the barracks were deblocked. I also said that I did hear about the blocking of the barracks in Varazdin and Bjelovar and the incident you mention now, this train composition, this trainload by which the military were pulling out its facilities, and that the train was blocked. I did hear about that, and I personally saw the withdrawal officers and their families as they were pulling out of the area of the 5th army area at the Bihac airport. There were columns and columns of officers with their families, carrying their own -- their furniture and property. They were waiting for planes to evacuate them from the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember a letter written by the deputy federal secretary for national defence, Admiral Stane Brovet - who was a Slovene, let me point out - on the 31st of August, 1991 which he sent to the president of the government of Croatia and spoke about the attempts and the famous looting that place over JNA property by members of the armed formations, armed units of the Croatian National Guard Corps and others? Do you remember that? That was quite public.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that now, but I know that there were attempts when officers' apartments were stormed and looted. I do know about that. There were rumours going round that things like that were happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that in all the armed conflicts by armed units from Krajina with the Croatian National Guard Corps and the JNA on the other side, until they had become the object of attack, their role was just to separate the two warring sides; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA units were deployed, according to the best of my information, as of the month of March. And the publicly declared reason was to separate the conflicting parties which were the DB and -- on the one side of Serbia and the Croatian police, which later became the Croatian National Guard Corps and its units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember the official announcement that was made by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, made public on the 28th of July, 1991, in which it states that with all cases - and I'm quoting from that report - in which the JNA units were forced to fire after the attacks by the MUP and the Croatian National Guard Corps was something that the public was informed about, when they had to return fire. It is common knowledge that the JNA units did not open fire on any occasion first and that members of the army and their families were subjected to very strong provocation. Their property was under jeopardy, and armed -- this finally led to armed attacks as well against their person. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I knew and the manner in which the escalation of the armed conflict came about, which means shooting on both sides, and usually this shooting came from the Krajina side. The police and DB shot at the Croatian police, and the Croatian police would respond, they would return fire, and then the Krajina police force or the volunteer units would attack the Croatian side by throwing mortars at them. The Croatian side would respond once again, and then the JNA would step in and open artillery fire. So that's what happened as of August 1991. Before that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that this is not correct, then, what it says here, that this is incontestable proof that the JNA units never opened fire first but that they opened fire exclusively to protect themselves once they had come under attack? Do you say that that is a lie?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you what you know -- I've said what I -- I'm telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of the events in Split that were well known on the 6th of May up until the 25th of July, that is to say when they lynched that soldier over there and launched demonstrations against the army in Croatia, that 126 cases of violence towards soldiers and JNA facilities were directed, as well as 22 armed attacks against JNA units, 11 cases where fire was opened on the barracks, 36 cases of unlawful action, and so on and so forth. All this was presented to the Yugoslav public. Now, do you claim that all that was pure fabrication?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say the following about that, and I've already spoken about that before this Tribunal: That after the events of the 2nd of May, especially after what took place in Borovo Selo, there was a great escalation of hate on the part of the Croatian population, the government, and the police. Intolerance generally, which -- and et cetera, and the role of the JNA in those conflicts. And I said that I attended public opinion and this expression of animosity and so on and that for days the victims from Borovo Selo were buried, public commemoration meetings were held, public protests and rallies were held over the events in Split, but the events escalated and there were more and more conflicts with the JNA, and the whole entire public was able to see this, when a citizen of Split in fact jumped up onto an armoured JNA carrier and strangled a young soldier in that truck -- tank. And a soldier was killed in Split. So this was the time of great escalation, when in Croatia a referendum was to be held as to whether the citizens of Croatia were in favour of a sovereign, independent Croatian or whether they wished to remain within Yugoslavia. It is my assessment that those events led up to the fact that the Croatian citizens for the most part opted for an independent, sovereign, and autonomous Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Does it emanate from what you're saying that the people of Krajina attacked the Croatians -- attacked Croatia and not that this new chauvinist regime in Croatia attacked the Serbs? What are you saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke quite specifically about what I knew, first of all in 1990, and then the political conflicts that ensued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be briefer, please. I can't keep listening to speeches. My question was quite specific. So you say the Krajina people attacked Croatia. Is that what you're claiming, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you how the conflicts came to take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: Your closest associates, were they the president of the Municipal Assembly of Donji Lapac, Slovastovac [phoen], and Vobrovac [phoen], Sergej Veselinovic? Were they your closest associates or amongst your closest associates? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rastovic was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly of Donji Lapac and president of the Assembly of North Dalmatia and Lika, the vice-president of the Serbian National Council, and vice-president of the Provisional Executive Council of SAO Krajina. He was the founder of the Serbian Democratic Party together with Dr. Jovan Raskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question was were they the -- your closest associates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were my political friends, my political comrades. We thought the same way up until the 29th of May, 1991, and then we went our own ways. They became a faction close to president -- Prime Minister Starevic and Martic. They were close to Frenki, and I can also say that they were his political associates and friends up until the formation of the government on the 29th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, we have here, written in hand, a letter, and I'm going to ask you to ask me [as interpreted] a few questions that these two men have written in their letter. They wrote the letter out in their own hands and signed it. They say: "We hope that you know that the Serbian Democratic Party obtained a nationalistic preface because we expected a political conflict at a national, Serbian, and Croatian level in Croatia and not because somebody from Serbia wanted that to happen but because, through its exclusively nationalist programme, it already puts by the HDZ."

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there was a political conflict between the representatives of the Serb people and the government of Croatia in 1990 and that you became involved in the conflict in the way in which I have described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they go on to say quite the opposite. They say what you're saying and that you're saying that somebody from Serbia was to blame. "We don't blame you because you didn't know about it," and you became a member of the SDS and League of Communists of Croatia later on. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why do they say? Fell into the SDS. I joined the SDS on the 17th of February 1990 at the founding Assembly, and I became a member because I was put forward by a member of the national board after a short introductory address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. They say: "But you know that at the party meetings that we held throughout the Krajina region we drew attention to the resurrection of the Ustasha movement and nobody influenced this from Serbia and you -" using the singular form - "are keeping quiet." That is what they are saying to you. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the meetings and events in 1990. I've spoken about them at length and quite specifically before this Tribunal already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says: "And we the undersigned" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you give us the date of that letter, the date of the letter from which you're quoting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just received it. Listening to this witness, these are his closest associates. They've just sent me this letter, Mr. Robinson. I just received it by fax. I have a whole series of letters from the people of Krajina with respect to the testimony of this witness of yours, and you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can tell you that your case will be strengthened if you are to call these people as witnesses, because the weight which the Chamber can attach to that kind of evidence will be limited, but it would be immeasurably strengthened if you were to call them as witnesses when you give your defence, so please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that advice, Mr. Robinson. Of course, these people who write letters and sign their own names to them are ready and willing to testify, because, so far, this has been a very amateur rigging of this whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. You're not making comments like that. Cheap sneers of that sort cut no ice at all. Now, you remember you're in a court and ask proper questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true what they say. "We, the undersigned, admired your rhetorical capabilities as to how you explained to the people the advent of the Ustasha fascist powers and how they would endanger them." They admired you for that. That's what they say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment by them of no relevance at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is this correct then: Do you not remember that the official authorities in Serbia at the time, via the Krajina generals, supported the side that was opposed to us, Racan's SDP party, and that is why the SDS, at later elections, did not win elections in the Serb Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. municipalities? How, then, is a plot and coordination as to some sort of forming of the Serb programme? Those are their words. What --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they're the ones that are asking the question. Do you remember that the official powers at the time supported Racan's party, which was in fact the League of Communists of Croatia and later on become the SDP at those particular elections?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't support Racan, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they're reminding you of that. That's what they say in their letter.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not support Racan at all. I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. I don't claim anything.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as far as this group of pensioned, retired generals is concerned, from Lika, I did hear about that, that they were in the pre-electoral campaign in 1990, that they went around in helicopters, supporting the leftist option, as they called it, of the League of Communists of Croatia, the left-wing Racan party, as you referred to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And they said, "Of course we didn't let Tudjman put a noose around our necks. We worked round -- with the organs of the municipalities, of which you were the president, for the forming of the Serbian National Association, and you know that nobody from Serbia took part in that. You know that very well." That is what they are writing to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke very specifically about those events, and I mentioned you for the first time where -- about the fact that you left to Kupari, to go to Kupari, and the first time I talked to you on the 11 of August, 1990. And I said at the SDS founding Assembly, I don't remember there were people from Serbia. Kosta Carlski [phoen] was the main guest there on behalf of the Democratic Party. I don't remember the others. Now, I don't know what the question is. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They say it was just our political battle with the nationalist Croatian authorities, our resistance to the disenfranchisement of the Serbian people and the abolishment of its constitutional rights on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our political battle, along with your guarantees that Yugoslav People's Army would protect our political struggle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they go on to say: "Did we not see through their attempts to deprive us of our status of a constituent nation and therefore taken political steps to protect ourselves?" That's what they say.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did talk about this political conflict and our political efforts to stand up to the amendments to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia where those rights were reduced and that we were opposed to the passing of a new constitution for Croatia in December which did not recognise the right of the Serbs as a constituent peoples and that we strove to ensure that those Serb rights should be defined in the Croatian constitution, and the Serbian autonomous province be recognised. And Raskovic was opposed to this notion of a county or Zupanja. And I can recall very well when I proposed that it be called the SAO autonomous province that he was very angry to have this word "Zupanja" or "county" introduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking about that. Yes, he was angry. But as you were the close associate with him, with these two, is what they say in their letter correct? And they say the following: "You say the nights we spent in the Knin centre for information, our courageous running towards every barricade that was under threat, during all that, with your presence you encouraged and supported the people of Krajina who trusted you unreservedly. Did you see anyone from Serbia there at the time?"

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the barricades, I explained how it came about that they were put up. As for the referendum --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was anyone from Serbia there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the barricades?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Was it someone from Serbia who put up the barricades?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see you at the barricades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I saw anyone from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have had testimony here --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to finish. I saw Jovica Stanisic with Milan Martic in May, 1991 and Martic introduced him as a person from the MUP of Serbia. That was in August 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did not someone from the MUP of Serbia have the right to be friends with someone and to cooperate with someone? Is that something that is suspect and inadmissible?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Martic was an inspector, he was not a Minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you comment on this passage in their letter? The Defence council that you are accusing of being a parallel power and body is something that you yourself set up until the Territorial Defence could be established. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. The so-called staff - I only heard it called a staff, not a council - was set up in the village of Padjeni on the 18th -- no, sorry, on the 16th -- just a moment, please. On the 18th of August, 1991, on the initiative of Marko Dobrijevic, Branko Perica, Zelenbaba, Opacic, and Martic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't explain this. They say that you set up this body that you're accusing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there at the beginning of the meeting but then I went off with Veljko Popovic, who was the president of the council of the municipality of Knin, to a meeting with Ante Bujas who was the chief of police in Sibenik and who was in charge of the Knin police station. And while this meeting at Padjeni was going on, I was with Bujas at the police station in Knin. At that meeting, Bujas asked that we agree to his proposal that 30 MUP policemen of Croatian ethnicity should arrive in the police station in order to improve the ethnic make-up. I wasn't there at the meeting until the end, so I don't know exactly how it ended. I know that the staff was established. Martic informed me of this on the following day. He invited me to Golubic, and I arrived in Golubic and he asked -- he said, "Will you tell us who will hold what post?" And I joked with him. I said, "Well, you can be the chief and Jovo can take charge of political activities, and Dusan Zelenbaba can be in charge of the medical corps, I'm sure he's familiar with that kind of work." And then Zelenbaba said, "Well, I never even completed my army service." And we laughed. This was a kind of a joke. Well, anyway, this was supposed to be a group that was called in aid to the barricades, but a few days later, it turned to a military camp and I didn't like this at all. They referred to my authority. They said that I had established and that this was a sort of staff of mine, and I asked to the late Jovan Raskovic to disband this staff at the SDS meeting, and this was done, as far as the staff is concerned. As for the Council of National Resistance, I did not take any part in that. That was an illegal organisation. And I said to the people whom I knew to be in it and who were causing incidents and making announcements over Radio Knin, all of which contributed to disorder and to the situation of chaos that prevailed, as the later academician Mr. Raskovic said, the purpose of this all was to be -- to introduce a state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're answering in too great detail. Be brief, please. They say that you yourself set up this body. They say it's not correct that you were there at the beginning of the meeting and then you left. They're lying, are they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are two bodies. One was the staff set up at the party meeting in Padjeni and the other body was the National Defence Council which they established, and I had no part in that and asked for it to be disbanded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they are writing here and saying why are you disgracing us with lies? We all breathed as one, fighting for our elementary right to life. And they say now you're saying that you were in some kind of conflict with all of them; that they were extremists and that you were a peacemaker.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying what happened. I was leading a political struggle which I described here in detail, and I can go on to explain it more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you say that what was in your heart and in your mind differs from what you were saying. Did you want to remain in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to achieve autonomy in Croatia, hoping that Croatia would remain within Yugoslavia. That's what I thought and what I said. I said that I felt the dismemberment of Yugoslavia as if it was the dismemberment of my own body, and I described in detail what happened later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, since you have now lifted the embargo on your testimony, the public will be able to see your entire testimony and the tapes where you are talking to the investigators and the representatives of the opposite side, and they will be able to see for themselves what this looks like. Your close comrades ask you is it not an insult to the Serbian people of the Krajina, our former friend, for you to consider them to be immature politically, to have been manipulated by someone, as if there had been no collective memory of the fascist and genocidal Ustasha state. They say who was it who manipulated our fathers, who experienced the Ustasha pogrom in 1941?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This all sounds like political comments and that sort of thing. It's not at all helpful. Let's move on. If you've got something concrete to put out of the letter, of course you can, but putting their comments and political views are totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. They go on to say: "For God's sake, what does this have to do with Serbia?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm going to stop this. You've either got some proper questions to ask or the cross-examination is coming to an end. This letter involves questions which are not proper or relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. We have to hurry up. I will pass over some questions because I think we have cleared up how the attack on the JNA went and the blockades of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that the army, at the price of unprecedented humiliation, avoided using any sort of drastic means to unblock the barricades; that they kept negotiating, that they kept trying to settle this peacefully? You heard the tape of the conversation between Kadijevic and Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the JNA used the most drastic and the strongest means at their disposal; the artillery and even the aviation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they used aviation to defend some transports that were attacked, that's true, but what you are saying is a complete lie. You say that they used the most drastic means. Do you know that the life of the members of the JNA, some of whom spent two and a half months under conditions of siege and blockade, do you know what it was like?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that the conditions were terrible, and I also heard something from the taped conversation between Hadzic and Mladic which Mladic let me hear when the Maslenica Bridge was taken. Hadzic was speaking of the difficult situation of the people in the garrisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In Varazdin, Jakova [phoen], Slavonska Pozega, Cakovec, they soon surrendered, almost without a struggle. They were under a blockade. Others, such as Bjelovar, Zagreb, Bosjic [phoen], Sibenika, Karlovac, Gospic offered strong resistance. They fought for as long as they could or, that is, until they were deblocked.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Tudjman's forces took over most of the garrisons in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Major Tepic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bjelovar was the only place with great sacrifices. After fierce fighting which lasted all day, the barracks fell, and Major Tepic died a heroic death, as did the commander of the Armoured Brigade. There was a brutal attack on the garrison. They had not attacked anyone at all. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, and Major Tepic has been declared a hero.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware of the fact that, in parallel to everything that was going on, as early as 1990 and 1991, ethnic cleansing took place where the Serb population was forced to move out, and they set out towards Serbia? Do you know that we had a hundred thousand refugees? Can you tell me exactly when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1991, Yugoslavia still existed. I know that during 1991, especially in the summer during the armed clashes in Eastern Slavonia, there were many refugees. I visited the village of Vajska myself on the Vojvodina side of the Danube, and I saw with my own eyes that there were large numbers of refugees accommodated in the school in Vajska, and they went to other parts of Serbia as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were the Prime Minister at the time. Do you know that a hundred thousand Serbs fled from Croatia, faced with unprecedented terror, with murders, arrests, people being taken away and going missing without any trace?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was a hundred thousand, but large numbers of people left Slavonia, and this was the first great exodus when the JNA retreated from there. This was a large exodus of the Serbs in the autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that even The New York Times in 1993 -- David Binder wrote in The New York Times of 10.000 Serbian houses that had been blown up and the expulsion of the Serbs from Croatia outside the area of the Krajina and that it was ethnically the purest country in Europe on the territories it controlled? It did not then control the area of the Krajina. They said there were a hundred thousand houses that were blown up. Granic admitted to 7.000.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, I belonged to the group of Serbs, a large group of Serbs who fled from that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I am speaking of the houses blown up in 1993, not 1995. Don't mix things up.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this? He wrote this in 1993, but this happened throughout this period. Do you know what was done in Zadar, what was done in other places? You mention that people were blown up, houses with whole families in them.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was talk of a Serbian family with the last name of Zec who were murdered in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you then trying to reduce these hundred thousand family homes to the Zec family alone, which is, of course, a tragic event? I'm speaking of 10.000 houses that were blown up in 1991, by the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but there were tens of thousands of refugees, mostly from Western Slavonia, which until then, had been held by the JNA. And before that, part of the area of the Slavonska Pozega municipality, there were houses that were burnt where the Croatian authorities had moved people out. These were villages on the western side of Slavonska Pozega. This happened in 1991. I have said that in the summer of 1991, a large number of people from Eastern Slavonia crossed the river Danube.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's not waste time on this, but was The New York Times influenced by this parallel structure you keep referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it not seem to you, Mr. Babic, that you are overly-eager to attack the parallel structure? Doesn't it seem to you that one can easily spot the empty gap in this mosaic which you will fill with someone you attacked from this so-called parallel structure in order to confirm the truth of what you are saying? Doesn't this whole testimony seem amateurish, all this fabrication?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is only one. It's not piecemeal. I'm saying what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain that on the tapes the innumerable tapes from your examination-in-chief by the Office of the Prosecutor, starting with the first tape which should be the beginning, you -- they say that in your previous interviews, you concluded this or that. Were you rehearsing your testimony, then? Was that a dress rehearsal? How many hours did you spend before the interview was taped, preparing for this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for my statement, I can say that I gave it according to the proper procedure. When the video and audiotapes had already started recording, that's when I started making my statement. Before that, I had contacts and two meetings with a member of the investigating team of the Tribunal. The contacts were five or ten minutes long when I asked for an interview and when we were scheduling the interview. So that's what we talked about, not the content of the interview. There were no previous interviews about what I was going to say. I did not discuss this with anyone, including representatives of the Tribunal, as regards the interview that was taped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the examples of Kijevo, Drnis, and so on that you mentioned and that you were asked about which the lady who conducted your examination-in-chief, you explained a certain setup. You say the DB provoked, the army attacked, expelled the Croats, and so on and so forth. So each of these events, Kijevo, Drnis, Oborovo, Obrovac, Kostajnica, Plaski, Skabrnja, Rupe, Nadin, Slunj, Ogulin, Saborsko, Petrinja, Sisak, Korenica, Dubica, there is information on each of these places, and all this information contradicts what you said in order to support this false indictment.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about what I know and about the events of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you see that what you knew then was one thing and that what you learnt later was another?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always gained information through personal inspection and obtaining information immediately after the events had taken place, and my information comes from several sources. This is not enough --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm stopping you, Mr. Milosevic. It's time for the break. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there is a request from the interpreters for both you and the witness to slow down so that they've got time to interpret properly. So remember, as I said at the outset, leave a gap, if you would, between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May, though I see I only have another hour left, but I shall do my best to bear in mind the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I've listed all these places, and reports that I have about them are quite opposite to what you have said. Tell me, please, do you have any subsequent information, perhaps, about a series of other crimes that occurred and which you are now denying? Let me list just a few. On the 22nd of August, 1991, the National Guards Corps and the MUP of Croatia rushed through the Serbian villages of Banija, Trnjani, Ckalja, Kinjacka, Bestrma, Plinski Put, Plinska Greda, Brdjani, and opened fire at anything that moved and killed dozens of people. Do you know about that or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You refer to what I'm saying as my pattern, but it is what I know about the way you waged the war. You drew the Serb people in Krajina into that war, the JNA into that war, to achieve your political goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you a specific question. Let's leave those speeches aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first part of your question. Secondly, from that period of time, I remember I was told about the killing of a large number of people in Kinjacka, near Sisak, where the Croatian armed forces killed a large number of Serbs in this village of Ninsko [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Sisak, which was not a part of Krajina and that was under Croatian authority. Do you remember in the summer and autumn 1991 dozens of Serbs were executed and dozens of bodies have still not been found? People were killed in their homes, in the street, at work, and in most cases, they were taken away to pre-arranged spots and liquidated there. This is Sisak. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many people were killed in Sisak, but I do know that a large number of people did flee from Sisak. I know that among them were four leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party who fled from Sisak and the whole area of Banija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that in the Pakracka Poljana there were large-scale liquidations of Serbs, in Marino Selo and Pakracka Poljana that started on the 9th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard about the events in Pakracka Poljana and Marino Selo where certain armed formations of Croatia committed crimes against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about these numerous small death camps that were formed there; Ribarska Koliba, Stara Ciglana, in Pakracka Poljana?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about Pakracka Poljana and Marino Selo. As for the other locations you mentioned, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many hundreds of Serbs were killed there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that a large number of Serbs were killed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that in Gospic that again you're quite erroneously describing the events of the 10th of September, 1991, where the Croatian guards and the MUP were grouping round the barracks and the military facilities in Kaniza? They switched off the electricity, water, and telephone cables and started killing soldiers outside the barracks and then opening fire from the hospital and the church, killing captain Miodrag Ostojic, Lieutenant Dusko Masinjamin [phoen], six soldiers were seriously wounded with shots fired into the compound.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember at the same time some officers were saying that the wives of officers, of Croat officers, were being hanged, and this was happening in Gospic. I also heard that there were murders of Serbs in Gospic who were buried somewhere around Gospic. There was an investigation and trials in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about this building Oglovnica that members of MUP and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the guards broke into? There was Milan Rozic known as Ruke [phoen], Matija Marte, known as Ivan; Podje [phoen] called Ziga, Zejlko; Petri Miroslav, and they executed -- took away and executed several dozen men of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Where did you say this occurred?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was in Gospic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't know the details about that. I do know that there were such events, and I've already said what I had heard about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that on the 25th of December, in a period of two days, 123 persons of Serb ethnicity were taken away from Gospic and Karlobag and executed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had heard that in that period of time and later a large number of Serbs were persecuted by the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember -- do you remember when patrolling No Man's Land near Siokakula [phoen], members of the TO and the JNA came upon carbonated bodies of 15 men and nine women?
