utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was told about that event. Charred bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that also in Karlovac, which you describe again quite wrongly, that on the 21st of September they stopped vehicles and killed the soldiers? Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the event at Goranski Most when Croatian forces stopped a group of reservists from the area of Kordun who were going to the barracks, Logorunska, a barracks near Karlovac, and they were killed on the bridge. One man managed to escape by jumping into the river. Yes, he jumped into the river, and he wrote about it, and I read his articles about the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They first shot at their feet, then they slit their throats, broke their bones, cut off their ears, all on this bridge.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read what this man wrote, that they forced them to lie on the ground, and they executed them one by one, and that he saved his life by jumping and escaping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the event in Paulin Dvor near Osijek? The inhabitants didn't even take up arms because they were given guarantees by the Croats from the neighbouring villages that nobody would harm them. However, when the police forces arrived in those villages, they put them all into two houses, and in the night between the 11th and 12th of December, they executed all the people in -- detained in house 51. In the morning, there were none of them dead or alive, there was just blood all over the building. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The body of Dara Vujanovic only has been found. There is no trace of the others to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness cannot give any evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, these investigators of the opposite side, in 2002, discovered the bodies of 18 missing from Paulin Dvor at a location called --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to stop you. You're asking this witness questions. It's only what he can give evidence about which is relevant at the moment. You can call evidence about these events if you wish. There's no point asking him about things he doesn't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In view of what was happening in Western Slavonia with the first major exodus of Serbs from Western Slavonia, how can you be saying what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you justify the Croatian authorities when you're aware of the exodus from Western Slavonia and of all these crimes that I have listed? Did you again subsequently come to the conclusion that it was the Serbs who attacked them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not attacking anyone or blaming anyone. I'm talking about specific events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that tens of thousands of Serbs on tractors and horse-drawn carts left Daruvar, Grubisno Polje, Podravska Slatina, a part of Pakrac in which they had had the majority otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The moment when the Yugoslav People's Army started withdrawing from those areas. I heard and listened, the people saying that rumours were spreading that the Ustasha, as they called the Croatian army, were slaughtering all over. I don't know exactly what was happening, but tens of thousands of Serbs withdrew together with the JNA from Western Slavonia. They fled. So I know what I heard and what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was not because of the crimes that were being committed. I asked a question to a colleague of yours who was a protected witness, and I asked him whether he knew that 193 settlements were ethnically cleansed, and he said that the figure wasn't right. It wasn't 193 but 163. That 52.320 Serbs left the area, and the final report mentions a figure of up to 70.000. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that tens of thousands of people from the area of Western Slavonia fled in the way I have described, when the JNA withdrew. If you want my opinion about it, that is also a consequence of your policies towards the Serbs and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Babic. And is it true that in Nos Kalic on the 3rd of April 1992, the Croatian army attacked this purely Serbian village and that today there are neither houses nor people? The entire village has been razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 3rd of April, 1992. Nos Kalic does not exist today. There are no houses or people there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the Croatian army was -- first captured the village of Nos Kalic, the only Serb settlement on the Miljevicka plateau, and razed it to the ground. There are no inhabitants there. Whether they were chased out or killed, I don't know. But in the next operation of the Croatian army, as it advanced along the Miljevicka plateau, in June 1992, several dozen members of the Territorial Defence of Krajina were killed in the area, and they were mostly from the area of Dalmatinsko Kosovo or Knin. This was the second advance of the Croatian army towards what were later known as pink zones, that is, territories that were not under UN protection, that were not protected under the Vance Plan that you accepted. So they were not protected by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're surely not going to deny that this treacherous attack in the pink areas which were zones, after all, in which nothing should have taken place that was like a military conflict, that all this happened in the presence of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were areas that were not under protection, because you didn't want the Vance Plan to be modified so that they would be protected as well. These areas were subsequently called the so-called pink areas after those events, and they were given that name so as to find a model that would be acceptable between the government of Krajina, you, and the Croatian side as to the establishment of Croatian authority there as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that they threw the dead Serbs into pits and on top of them large rubbish to cover up traces of their crimes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many victims were discovered as a result of this attack and conflict between the Croatian army and the Territorial Defence or, rather, the Serbian army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, as it was called by then, and a number of bodies, I think, were never found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're also distorting the events in Maslenica on the 22nd of January, 1993 when the Croatian army attacked the Republic of Srpska Krajina in the south from Zadar towards Benkovac and Obrovac, and also from Sinj towards Vrlika.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you talking about, sir? What have I distorted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that on 22nd of January the Croatian army attacked the Republic of Serbian Krajina from the south, from the direction of Zadar, and also from Sinj towards Vrlika? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two attacks by the Croatian army that followed one another. The first was in the area of the Maslenica Bridge, the Ravni Kotari area, along the Adriatic motorway, and the Croatian forces then captured a part of the territory that was under the so-called protection of the UN but which was not demilitarised. The immediate cause for the attack, actually, was that the agreements around the opening of the so-called blue routes had not been implemented. This is -- was agreed between the government of Krajina with the Croatian authorities and your support. Why this wasn't implemented, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean why I didn't realise it? What are you talking about? Tell me, is quite the opposite true, quite the opposite, that it was only then that since they were attacked in the parts that they were protected by UNPROFOR, the people of Krajina took from the warehouse heavy weapons in order to protect themselves from the attacks as UNPROFOR did not protect them? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is true that you did not respect the plan you had signed. There wasn't complete demilitarisation, there wasn't a mixed police force, and that the displaced Croats did not return. And it is true that the Croatian army attacked the area on the date you have given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, regarding the Medak pocket, south-east of Gospic, was that also a treacherous attack after the UN were protecting the area for 18 months? People were not expecting any kind of attack. They had been under protection for 18 months by tanks and infantry on Divoselo, Pocitelj.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that in the area, the Croatian army committed a massive crime against the Serbian civilian population. A large number of members of the Serbian army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina were killed in that attack. The area -- this event occurred under conditions of open hostilities in 1993, in between -- between the Serbian army of Krajina and the Croatian army. This area was also a UN protected area and it is a fact also that the area was not demilitarised, that you did not demilitarised it under the provisions of the Vance Plan that you imposed on us, and it is a fact also that there was an armed conflict between the Croatian army and police on the one hand and the Serbian forces on the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the truth quite the opposite, that the citizens believed in UNPROFOR protection, that they were surprised by the attack, and that unheard-of crimes were committed, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot mourn more for the people who died then than I did, but the fact is that there was an armed conflict at the time between the Serbian army of Krajina and the Croatian army. You said that the conflict occurred in January 1993, and that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the written report by General Jean Cot, who was the commander of UNPROFOR at the time, dated the 19th of September, 1993, once he had toured the villages? He said, and in his report he states, and I quote the report: "I did not find any traces of life, any signs of life, either of people or animals, in several villages through which we passed. The destruction is complete, systematic, and intentional." Do you remember that report of his?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is absolutely correct and corresponds to the same picture that the armed formations of the JNA and other people under its command made in 1991 in certain areas of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this, whereas that repetition of yours, your constant repetition of the accusations is not an answer to my question. What I'm asking you is this, and please just answer my questions --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that the way in which Franjo Tudjman waged a war in 1993 and 1995 against the Serb people in Krajina is the same as you waged via the Yugoslav People's Army against the -- against Croatia and the Croatian people in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that these crimes that were perpetrated during all the operations, for example, the Flash and Storm operations, that the army did that, that I did that in 1991 against the Croats? What Croatian territories were rid of Croats and which Croats were killed and everything that you are saying, all these territories emptied of them? And you're speaking about the actions of the JNA against Croatian territories. What territories are those?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I stated very specifically what the armed formations of the JNA did under its command and under your Supreme Command, what they did in 1991. I mentioned all the villages; Kijevo --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, nobody died in Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Drnis. I mentioned the area of Vuksic and the area around Benkovac and Maslenica, the Maslenica bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you allow me to finish, please. You asked me, so let me finish. In Saborsko, Slunj, Kostajnica, around Mitosevac [phoen] which means -- actually, I also mentioned before this Tribunal all these areas which were destroyed under your Supreme Command in 1991. In 1995, in the Flash and Storm operations in Western Slavonia and SAO Krajina, the armed formations of Croatia did the same against the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are comparing deblocking the road in Kijevo in which nobody was killed, deblocking the road through Saborsko because you weren't able to be linked with other areas - and we had a witness here who took part in the Saborsko operation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not a proper question. This is argument again, Mr. Milosevic. You're putting your arguments. You can put them to us. It's not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that that is the same as the Flash and Storm operations and the expulsion of 250.000 Serbs from Krajina; is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's precisely the point that I was making. Yes. Go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. Is it true that in the negotiations with Nikolic that the motorway was opened, that you closed it and the Croatian forces used this as a pretext to use violence and tanks to open the motorway?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The motorway was closed by Milan Martic, was blocked by Milan Martic, the former president of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and I was the Foreign Minister at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you remember that by Resolution 994 of the 17th of May, 1995, the UN Security Council demanded that Croatia pull out of the areas under UN protection, that it had come to that? Of course, without any sanctions towards Croatia, but they even had to request that this be done. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember and I said that via the civilian representatives of the UN, I discussed this issue with them, with the UN representatives. However, Croatia retained control over the Okucani region which it had taken in the Flash operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how many people were killed in the Flash and Storm operations? How many were expelled?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but dozens of -- I don't know the exact figures. In the Storm operation, what was expelled or the people that took refuge, according to what I know and my assessments, is between 200 and 240.000 Serbs in the Storm operation, Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's remain there, because quite obviously you have your own approach to all these issues. But let's go back for a moment, as we're in open session, after the operation, Operation Storm, you came to see me for a talk of some kind, and you said that it lasted for just several minutes, and that before that you had been to see Mirko Marjanovic, and you said that I had told you that we're going to send the refugees to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you -- you said you would put up 100.000 in Kosovo and that a large number of others, that is to say the rest, could go to Republika Srpska. And when I asked you whether we could go to Eastern Slavonia, your answer was, "No, not for now."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not true, but let me just ask you about the facts. Let's stick to the facts. Do you know that in Serbia, after Operation Storm and in view of what was going on in the Republika Srpska, in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, there were 1 million refugees?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information and my assessments, there were approximately 800.000. Between 800.000 and 1 million refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ah, a million refugees.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assessment was 800.000 refugees after the events that took place in Kosovo, after the war in Kosovo. That means 800.000, maybe up to 1 million. There were refugees in Serbia and Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you talking about the war in Kosovo? I'm asking you about after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 600 to 800.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were 1 million refugees at the time in Serbia. Do you happen to know that in Kosovo the total was only 10.000 refugees, just 10.000 refugees in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for certain there were less than 100.000 because they couldn't have been put up there. So many people couldn't have been accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course they couldn't have been accommodated there. But far under the -- below the percentage, because 1 per cent of the refugees which existed in Serbia were in Kosovo, and this represents 10 per cent of the territory Serbia, Kosovo does. So it was ten times below average. That was the figure of refugees in Kosovo province. Are you acquainted with those facts and figures?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is why we were astonished when you said that 100.000 people would be put up in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, did you go to Marjanovic for a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Marjanovic tell you that we would receive all the refugees?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said the following -- would you allow me to answer your question, please? He said the following: He stated that he would accept and take in all those who came to Serbia but first that people could be accommodated with their relations if they were the immediate family; father, mother, brother, sister, children, et cetera. All the others would be escorted. They would be under escort, police escort, and under the control of the staff you set up, Jovica Stanisic, nicknamed Badza, he was the Communications Minister, and one other man, I can't remember his name, they would all be displaced and settled around Serbia, according to your plan. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he mention them going to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said those two things to me. He didn't say where they would be put up but in what way they would be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it logical to assume that when 250.000 people are coming in, a staff be set up, a headquarters, to settle them all over Serbia because Belgrade would not be big enough to fit them all in? Wouldn't that be logical?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Belgrade is concerned, according to my information you did not permit people to turn off the main road and come into Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were an enormous number of refugees in Belgrade itself.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew, the only way people could go to Belgrade was if they had any immediate relations there, close family, or if they fled from the column and left it secretly, without the permission of the police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it logical that a government and its staff should gear the refugees to an equal distribution over Serbia? Serbia is not large enough to be able to take all the refugees into its capital city.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, you did not permit refugees to be put up in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because there was sufficient numbers in Belgrade already. So what do you want to say about that? The fact is that the police -- you said that the police escorted the columns --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to bring this argument to an end. He's given his answer as far as he knows. Now, you can call evidence about it if you wish, but he can't take the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained to us in this courtroom that I wanted to put the refugees up in Kosovo province according to some sort of secret plan that I had. I'm now going to show you the Official Gazette of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, a copy of the Official Gazette, so not of Serbia but of Yugoslavia, and the date is the 9th of February, 1990, which was the time when Yugoslavia was an integral country, a whole country, and when the president of the Yugoslav state Presidency was Janos Djezjenovcek [phoen], when the Federal Assembly had a Chamber of Nationalities, and when it had the Executive Council, the Federal Council, and when that Federal Council of Yugoslavia, the federal Executive Council, way back in 1990, enacted a certain -- a set of conclusions that were made public in the Official Gazette in Yugoslavia which speaks about Kosovo, that they introduced unrest and insecurity among all the peoples there, the Serbs and Montenegrins in the first place, that the exodus from Kosovo had been stepped up and that measures were being taken for their own personal safety and the safety of their property, and that aggressive action on the part of the Albanian separatists and terrorists should be prevented and stopped. All this is what the Assembly says, the Assembly of the Socialist Federal Republic says in 1990, and points out the continuous activities of Albanian separatists and terrorists geared towards separating Kosovo from the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia and the conclusions it makes is the following: It says that the programme is a democratic document, and then it publishes the title The Yugoslav Programme of Measures and Activities to Stop the Exodus of Serbs and Montenegrins from the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo, the speedier return of those people who have already left the province, and the arrival of all those who wish to live and work in Kosovo province. So what, then, is this secret plan about Kosovo that you're talking about and my personal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't recollect any talk of a secret plan, but we'll ask the witness about that. Did you understand there was a secret plan of some sort to resettle people in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish. Let him clarify it. Let him clarify. You're putting it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that in the course of -- I don't think that I spoke about this issue in the course of my testimony in that particular fashion. I think that previously, perhaps when I spoke to the investigators, I happened to mention that I knew that the government of Serbia did have a plan to resettle 1.000 people returning to Kosovo in that sense, but I don't -- didn't speak about any secret, covert plan. I just brought it up when I was thinking about the population, the way in which the refugees were put up and accommodated, resettled and so on. So this was knowledge I gained from the media at the time. I don't think I spoke about any secret plan. I just happened to mention what I heard about. I heard of the existence of a plan, whether it was a Serb plan or a plan of the government of Serbia to have 1.000 Serbs settle in Kosovo, rather re-settle in Kosovo province, people who were going back, something along those lines, but I don't think I brought this up in this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I read out this Yugoslav programme and activities to stop the exodus of Serbs and Montenegrins and the speedy resettlement of people who had left, and to enable anybody who wanted to go to Kosovo province to live and work would be allowed to do so. This is an Official Gazette adopted by the Assembly of Yugoslavia, the programme contained in it. You can have it because I don't want witnesses of this kind to manipulate facts and all subsequent witnesses that are going to appear here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That -- that is not a proper comment about the witness at all. But you'd like this exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many on the territory of Croatia were camps for Serbs? Let me refresh your memory. For example, do you know that there were 221 camps for Serbs on Croatian territory in Biograd na Moru, three in Bjelovar, nine -- three in Varazdin, three in Bikovski [phoen], one in Virovitica, three in Vrginmost, two in Glina, Vrpolje one, in Goli Otok, and so on and so forth. And 221 camps for Serbs in all. That was the total figure.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in -- around Bjelovar and in Slavonia after the Flash operation, Operation Flash, a large number of camps were set up by the Croatian authorities, and they put the detained Serbs in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the document now. Mr. Milosevic, it's a lengthy document. No doubt it deals with a lot of other matters which have nothing to do with this trial. If the first three pages were translated, is that going to be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can have it translated in its entirety. This would show you that the whole of Yugoslavia and -- took steps to stand up to the intentions, as it says here, of Albanian separatists and terrorists, and that was way back in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But does the whole document deal with that issue or does it go on to deal with other issues?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just the programme which relates to Kosovo, Mr. May. There's nothing else there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We'll give it an exhibit number and it will be translated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Defence Exhibit 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that there is an association of former camp inmates of 1991, the president of which is Petar Pjodorov?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says that the Serbs for camps [as interpreted] was set up in April 1991, that early. Is that correct? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any concrete facts and figures from 1990 -- 1991, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says that it is assumed that 5.000 persons, women and children, were held in custody in Croatia. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that people were imprisoned, but I don't have any precise facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says in September the Black Legion arrived and their behaviour was brutal. They beat people, stamped on them.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this Black Legion. I know of the Black Legion from World War II.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Sisak there were 400 men, women, and children imprisoned alone. Do you know that? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no specific figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Lora camp in Split, 39 former members, former soldiers of the JNA were killed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in the prison in Lora, a large number of people were killed. They were abused and beaten by the Croatian army and police who were in command of the Lora prison, and I know that some people who were detained there -- I know some of the people who were there. I know their names and I know that UNPROFOR intervened to have them released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the inmates made statements to the effect that their ears had been cut off, they were tortured with electricity, they were forced to eat each other's ears, the ears that had been cut off. Their bodily parts had been cut off. I have several statements from the camp inmates. I haven't got time to read them all out. Were you ever interested in statements of this kind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about that, and I was interested in hearing about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it true, then? Are the facts correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard all the things that you have just mentioned as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that there are doctors' reports which show that a person was skinned alive, that people were skinned alive? Their skins were taken off their bodies while they were still alive; they were flayed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a court report on the examination of a detainee from Lora, and we can see on that basis that the warden, Tomo Dujic and Perisic, says that: "They took it out on us by mistreating us with electricity. They placed electrodes on our ears, and these were linked to transformers on the table, and this led to great pain. I thought my eyes would pop out of my sockets." That's what he writes. And do you know how many examples of this? Vestvic [phoen], a soldier from Klagovac [phoen] was killed in Lora, having tortured him severely before that. And Jelic Dusko, a reservist from Trebinje, also died as a result of the beatings. So you have heard about the Lora prison, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and I know some of these people personally from Civljani and Poljani who were taken prisoner in 1994 in the Operation Storm and put in prison in Lora. I heard about others too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can refresh your memory. I can supply you with a list of these, but I'll leave that for later on. I have a list of persons who disappeared in the Lora prison, but we have to hurry up. Is it true that in the late afternoon hours of the 2nd of August, 1995, from the government bureau in Belgrade on Terazija Square you established telephone links with a member your delegation who was at the Geneva negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the 3rd -- what did you say, the 3rd of August? Yes, on the 3rd of August talked to Milivoje Vojnovic and Milo Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that one of your ministers was with you on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who was with me then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was Mile Bosnic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile Bosnic was there very frequently. Whether he was with me at that particular time, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that a member of the delegation of the RSK on the other side of the telephone line informed you that the delegation in Geneva was met by a CIA representative and was told that the next day at the negotiations with Croatia they were not to accept anything and to refuse everything that was offered them? Is that correct? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard later on, and I think Milivoje Vojnovic told me, that there were two men who tried to prevail upon them not to accept the agreement. One of them was the Yugoslav Ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva, I've forgotten his name now, and the other man was somebody who allegedly had a Serb surname, but he -- Vojnovic said that he was in fact working for the CIA, and he too said that they should not accept the agreement, agree to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Can you tell me and the public in the public gallery, and especially the Serbian public following this, what was the task in Geneva of the representative of the CIA who met the delegation of Republika Srpska Krajina while you were sitting there talking to Ambassador Galbraith in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Ambassador Galbraith in Belgrade the day before. We discussed the Z-4 plan, the new mandate of UNPROFOR, the situation in Bihacki Zepa and the opening of the roads on that day. And the man you say was a CIA agent, they -- he did not meet them, they met him in private, and they said he was from the CIA, the Vojnovic, this man Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not saying that Vojnovic was a CIA agent.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I'm talking about. I'm talking about what Milivoje Vojnovic, a member of the delegation of the Republic of Srpska Krajina in Geneva told me about the events and the way in which negotiations were conducted in Geneva. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you deny in public here that you were aware on that occasion that the Clinton Administration was supporting the Croatian army in Operation Storm, not only verbally but also by providing logistic and other support?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ambassador of the USA, Peter Galbraith, the Ambassador to Zagreb told me he had the support of the American government for the Z-4 plan and what we were discussing. I don't know about the rest that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we agreed on about the Z 4 plan? Who agreed about the Z-4 plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting, I agreed to the Z-4 plan proposed by Peter Galbraith, the Ambassador of the USA in Zagreb, and he also mediated with Tudjman. He told me that he had the support of the US government and that this was a good plan for the Serbian Krajina and that he was mediating between the government of the Krajina and the Croatian government, that is Tudjman, in order to have the Z-4 plan implemented in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since I only have about 12 minutes left, let me just go into some of the intercepts, although some are doubtless doctored. Karadzic calls me Slobo. He never actually called me Slobo. And there are other details, a sort of frame or ram is mentioned. I don't know what this refers to, but look at this conversation. It's tab 44. It's a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic taped on the 23rd of November, 1991. He asks me whether some sort of meeting had gone well, and I said, "Yes, yes, it did go well." And then I quote the conversation. I'm quoting from the conversation you presented here. I say, "I think that man down there, that Babic, is swine." And then down here it says, referring to Marc Goulding, who seems to be a very descent Englishman, I'm just quoting now from what it says here, it says here: "He replied that he had talks yesterday with Mr. Babic who says he is..." and then there are three dots "said that these municipalities are under threat and he is not under threat. He doesn't need anyone. And Karadzic says, "Uh-huh." And I say, "He doesn't need anyone, but Franjo should run him down and his people over there should be slaughtered. I think he' a bastard." Of course I said that, and I don't want to discuss it now, because there's no point in dealing with maps now. We have to establish principles and the issue of maps is an issue of fact, and the fact referred to is where the people under discussion live, and that's the wording used by Ambassador Wayne, so where people live, where Serbs live, that's where the protected areas would be. And then on the 11th of December, that's tab 45 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you want now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- if you've got a question about tab 44, you should ask it, otherwise there's no point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, from these three conversations, let me quote a sentence from each of them and then I will put my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. While it's in the witness's mind, you were asking him about a number of these things and the witness should have a copy of them, by the way, Exhibit 353, tab 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it clear to you, Mr. Babic, that it was evident to me then that you were actually helping Tudjman with your vehement radicalism which went against the interests of the Serbian people in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was then asking for protection from the JNA, and everybody knows this. I wanted the JNA to remain there and protect the Serbian people until a political solution should be found. Secondly, your assessment and the way you referred to me, that says more about you than it does about me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in this second conversation, tab 45, I say, "This man is an idiot."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... has he got one? Tab 45. Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says, "I think that he is helping Tudjman on purpose, providing him with an excuse for this situation," that is for violence against the Serbs. And later it says: "It must be made public that we support this. It must be clearly seen. And this is the best evidence that we are in favour of peace." So you knew that I think and I thought, in the autumn of 1991, that you were playing into Tudjman's hands and giving him an excuse for what he was doing against the Serbs at that time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you're referring to this plan and an excuse for Tudjman, let me say the following: It was you and Tudjman who accepted this plan without asking us. You imposed this plan on the people of the Krajina. You failed to comply with this plan, and you prompted Tudjman's aggression against the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We shall be able to explain this easily. Look here. Here's another conversation. I will quote from it just to make it clearer that this was my position all along, and you are mentioned as a close associate of mine, so let everyone be clear about this. And this is tab 20. I apologise. Tab 20. 05 is the last number on the page. The first sentence says: "I don't know whether anyone can say something to him so that he will either quieten down or maybe he could be dismissed." And then, "He will do enormous damage, so that's all that can be done." Then this goes on to say: "The only card they have to play is Milan Babic, their only trump card," because you were doing what you were doing. This is my conversation with Karadzic. And he agrees with me, and as you yourself said, he tried to convince you to accept the Vance Plan. And he explained to you that the formula of peace was the best formula. Radovan Karadzic did this in my presence. And then I go on to say: "If someone had shot me, I would never have been able to imagine who Tudjman's trump card would be," and that was you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in 1991, you waged a horrific war. You dragged the Serbian people into that war. You did not protect the Serbian people. You brought shame upon the Serbian people. You brought misfortune on the Croatian people, the Muslim people, and ultimately the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm putting facts to you, Mr. Babic, and you can hold speeches which we can read in the papers from sources such as the ones you are involved with, but what I have read out to you is what your closest associates write to you, and the public can judge what is true and what is not true.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have been putting forward facts here for ten days now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you are living from one day to another and thinking only of your own pragmatic interests, is it clear to you that Croatia will have to give the Serbian people the status of a constituent nation again? Because the Krajina lasted much longer than the Paris commune. Do you think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now moving into present politics, and I don't think that is part of our trial at all. Now, if you've got any more questions about the relevant period, you can ask it, Mr. Milosevic. Five minutes remain. But current politics are not going to assist.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a pile of documents here submitted by you, but time does not allow me to go into them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You accused Martic of holding prisons in Knin. You said here that in those prisons Croats were tortured or mistreated. I don't know anything about anyone being tortured. According to all the statements I received, and this was confirmed by some of the witnesses and quoted by me, the Croats lived on an equal footing in Knin, even held posts, various posts. And in one of the documents you brought, there is an order here, Osman Vukic, a policeman from Zadar, is to be released. He had been arrested in Knin. This order was implemented immediately, and it was signed by the Prime Minister, Dr. Milan Babic. So you were the one who was able to release someone. So why then are you pointing the finger at Martic? If Croatia was in your heart and not on your lips and in your mind, so you released this man Osman Vukic, why did you not release them all if you knew someone was being tortured and mistreated? As you see, you had the authority to do this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Question. Question, Mr. Milosevic, now. Mr. Babic, would you like to answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already spoken of this document. It was not the norm for the Prime Minister to release someone from prison. This was one of three occasions when someone interceded with me from Zadar and Sibenik, some medical doctors, and I asked in the MUP in Knin that this be done, and they then asked me to sign such a document. But this was not the usual procedure. It was the police that ran the prison. They held prisoners there for a long time, and then they exchanged them for imprisoned policemen from the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why are you constantly using the third person singular when you should be using the first person plural when you -- for things that you should be held responsible for, although no one should answer before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only speaking of facts and of what I knew at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you keep referring to Martic's Police. This was the police of the Krajina. It was not Martic's private police. Did Martic had a private police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was your police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Babic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it tab 168 the accused is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Petar N. Stikovac? Do you know a man called Petar N. Stikovac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to a Professor from Licka Kaldrma, a teacher, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also sent in a statement, and he agreed to have this put in the defence, and he asks you, "Today all Serbs that are worth anything are either in their graves or in prison," and he's asking you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're not interested in the comments of letter-writers. It's totally irrelevant. Now, if there's a concrete fact you want to ask arising out of it, you can put it, but you can't put what's in the letter in terms of comment and the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since all this was my fault, listen to this order. Is it correct that even without asking Milan Martic you appointed him deputy commander of the Territorial Defence and declared yourself to be the commander? Is this correct? Here is the order on the appointment of the deputy commander of the Territorial Defence of the Krajina, Milan Martic. According to my information, you never even asked him if you could appoint him. You acted arrogantly and decided about everything, doing whatever you wanted, and now you are blaming Martic who, unlike you, is a decent man?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that I appointed him and it's correct that agreed to that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What tab, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tab 55 and the tab before was correct it was 168 as to what Judge Kwon said.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 352, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. It sounds about your last question. You may have time for two more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: ... addressed to me late January 1991. I don't have the tab here, but it's -- it bears a number, an ERN number, 02172108. It's a letter written by you addressed to me, and you say: "Pursuant to the conversation," I'll skip over the introductory part, "On the occasion of the negotiations between the representatives of the republics and especially the conversation that is to take place between you and the representative of Croatia to discuss the future ordering of -- of the state, we ask you that you receive the delegation of the Serbian National Council, because we wish to inform you of the views of the Serbian people Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. living in the Republic of Croatia and the area of the Serbian Krajina. We would be grateful if you could receive us before the 25th of January this year," signed by Prime Minister Dr. Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's tab 34 from Exhibit 352.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on a page, you are more or less asking me to instruct you as to what you should do. At the end of January 1991, you are asking me to receive a delegation of your National Council. I'm saying your because you were president of that council among the 32 other positions that you held during those five years in Krajina to present your views in connection with the forthcoming talks, because in those days, the presidents of the six republics were discussing future relationships in Yugoslavia. So isn't this in contradiction with your allegations about secret talks and discussions? The way in which this letter is addressed and the request to receive the Serbian National Council at the end of January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the sixth or seventh meeting with you which took place after that letter. I've already testified about that in this court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. As I have no more time, just one more question. And who could the Serbs from Krajina address for aid being exposed to all these dangers, including the danger to their very lives and existence, if not to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were the man that people trusted and I trusted. You were the man who persuaded us into the correctness of your views.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question is: Who else could they address but Serbia? Wasn't it logical? Was it a secret? Was it a secret that Serbia assisted you? Was that a secret and you're revealing the secrete here? We assisted you in every respect to survive.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You and your policies are the past. Your policy of nationalism, yours, Tudjman's and even mean should be relegated to the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. You will get an answer to your question. The question which the accused puts to you and perhaps you would answer it, Mr. Babic is this: Who else could they -- could you have turned to at the time but him? That's the point that he makes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one else. We only addressed him, and he promised protection, protected us, and then compromised that protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. No. We must bring this to an end. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I -- if you don't want, let me ask you another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Though the struggle for freedom will never be relegated to the past. As you do not remember anyone who was killed, I will leave for you lists of close to 5.000 men from Krajina, their names, place of birth, to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to you, gentlemen, I would like to make a gift of a book in Serbian and English speaking about the genocide of the Serbs, 1941, 1945, and 1991 and 1992, and if you just leaf through it, you may have perhaps an idea of what you are doing and of what is being discussed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These documents will be marked for identification. The list and the pamphlet will be given distinct numbers. They will not be admitted at this stage. We will hear any objections from the Prosecution, and then we will consider whether to admit them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, the exhibit numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the list will be marked for identification as D69, and the book will be marked for identification as D70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Babic, I shall do my best in this cross-examination on behalf of the amicus to address only facts and the evidence that has already been presented here, and I will ask you for some clarifications. So let me start first with what you've said on the 19th of November, 2002, and it is on page 12.976 of the LiveNote. You said the following, and I quote: That after the formation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in April 1992, through Lilic, Slobodan Milosevic had control over all federal institutions. I should just like us to clear up a few things in chronological order to assist the Court. First of all, I would like to know the following: Is it true that on the 27th of April, 1992, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established? Is it true that from the 27th of April, 1992, until the 15th of June, 1992, the position of president of that state was held by Branko Kostic? If you don't remember the date --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the first elected president by the Assembly of FRY was Dobrica Cosic, who performed the duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that it was Branko Kostic or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we come to the elections. Yes. On the 15th of June, the elected president was Dobrica Cosic, and he remained in that position until the 1st of June, 1993. And then for a brief time in June it was Milos Radulovic, and then Lilic from the 25th of June, 1993, until June 1997. So during the time of the events in Krajina, the indictment period, August 1991 to June 1992, Lilic did not hold any federal positions.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand you're talking about the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You mentioned Lilic in connection with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So he is mentioned in that connection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but he had no authority until 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, there was the war in Krajina, in 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm saying that he had no federal position during the time of the war in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had any connection at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the president of state.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, not the SFRY. Did I mention Lilic in the context of SFRY or FRY?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that as from 1992, Slobodan Milosevic controlled federal institutions through Lilic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said he had control over the federal institutions through Lilic as well. He was not the president, but he was one of the presidents of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us not waste time. In 1992, Lilic was not the Supreme Commander of the armed forces. He was not president of the country. He wasn't, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in 1992, but it was then that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established, and I mentioned Lilic in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's not dwell on that any further. Up until then, until the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established, the federal Presidency acted as the Supreme Commander. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of SFRY was the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the SFRY according to law. I said that over the rump Presidency, which was formally the Supreme Commander, the real Supreme Commander was Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is precisely why I'm asking you. The rump Presidency, in the most critical period, in March 1991, could not act. The rump Presidency, as you call it, was paralysed because decisions could not be taken to take certain steps in relation to paramilitary formations precisely because the Presidency was complete.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I said that in March there were changes in the members of the Presidency, and at the end of May 1991, the federal -- federal Assembly said who were the newly elected members. Branko Kostic, I said, Sejdo --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness be asked to answer my questions. I'm asking him about March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the 10th and 15th of March, was the federal Presidency in complete composition? When the vote of a Serb from Bosnia, the representative in the Presidency, it was decisive for certain measures not to be taken against paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. The Presidency did not agree to the army's demand for such measures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you have already said that Slobodan Milosevic controlled the rump Presidency. I won't go back to that. But as of March up until December, until he resigned as a member of the Presidency of the SFRY, Mesic obstructed the work of the Presidency. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've given a long period. I can't say yes or no. I think he was elected at the end of May, after obstruction in the Presidency, and then formally he was president of the Presidency until I don't know when. Until Croatia proclaimed independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. He resigned in December. My question is: Did he obstruct the work of the Presidency precisely so that the Yugoslav People's Army could not operate? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how Mesic behaved. I know what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the first point I wish to address. I should now like to go on to the next one. I would now like the document to be prepared. Tab 1, 352. It was the first exhibit which was tendered here. And it has to do with the programme of the Serbian Democratic Party. On the first day of the examination-in-chief, you confirmed that on the 17th of February, 1990, the Democratic Party was formed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was only three days after the 14th of February when the Assembly of Croatia adopted amendments to the constitution legalising the multi-party system. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you appeared to have been the first party to be formed in Croatia after the introduction of the multi-party system.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HDZ was formed but I don't know whether it was legal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and you became a member of that party and its functionary on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The programme of the party we are talking about, while you were working, did you support that programme throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it an expression of the spirit, the wishes, and needs of the people of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the political programme of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. In the first sentence of that programme, it says that your interests will best be defended by a general democratisation of the country. I would like you to have that programme in front of you for me to be able to ask you something about it. If you could confirm a few matters contained in that programme. Tab 1, Exhibit 352. In that programme and in answering the questions from the Prosecution, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Tapuskovic. We can't find the passage you are referring to in the tab 1. Could you check it once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English translation, it is page 11. And I shall exclusively be dealing with this chapter 3. Chapter 3, which talks about democratic federalism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you opted for a federative internal organisation of Yugoslavia in that programme.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the political option we supported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... isn't it out of Exhibit 351 instead of 352?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first exhibit tendered here. I thought it was 352. Yes. Yes. 351/1. I do apologise. I have it in my hands now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please, I wish to draw your attention to what it says on page 18.18. In the Serbian version, it is page 11, in the middle somewhere. And in the English version, it is point 18 on page 18. And it says: "The army remains Yugoslav. Its federative character includes a federative command and protection of the federal socio-political system." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on in that chapter, and this is on page 12 of the English translation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. We don't have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and it says as follows: "We are in favour of the equality of citizens proclaimed by the single-party system, because in that system, one Slovene citizen was equivalent in political evaluation to five Serbs." Does it say that? Does it say that in the translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the transcript there is a mistake. It says just the opposite. It says, "We are not in favour."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that not a good translation of what I was saying?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear -- misheard. The interpreters misheard. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It's time to adjourn in any event. We will return to this after the -- after the adjournment. We will adjourn for twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Please try and understand me. Ms. Higgins had a death in the family, and my assistant has had to leave, so I'm left here alone with all these piles of paper. So I will do my best to be as efficacious as possible in my examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'd like to draw Their Honours' attention to page 12 of the English translation, paragraph 1. The Exhibit number, as I've already stated, is 351/1. What we were discussing with the interpreters a moment ago, the sentence reads: "We are not in favour of civil equality..." Not in the affirmative, in the negative. Then the text goes on to state in the programme, and I do think that this does have significance and you'll say whether or not: "We are in favour of the principle of having one citizen, one vote." Is that the principle that you advocated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the principle of one citizen, one vote, throughout the entire history of Yugoslavia, was that principle a problem precisely because half the population of Yugoslavia, from 1918 and especially after 1941, was represented by the Serb population? The Serbs made up almost half the population of Yugoslavia, roughly half. Isn't that right? The Serbs made up half the population?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This principle of one man one vote was to be realised at the level of republics and federations. So these are two principles; one man, one vote. What are you asking historically? I'm not quite understanding you. What were you asking about history, the historical framework?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in Yugoslavia, half the population -- about half the population were Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about half. The Serbs were the majority nation, not half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean there were more than half, more than half the population were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me what period you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to 1945 onwards, for as long as Yugoslavia existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serb nation was the majority people, not 50 per cent but the majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I'm asking you. So there was no danger of a Greater Serbia but of this principle one man, one vote in that setup in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the democratic principle stated here, the basic democratic principle in a democratic society. I don't understand what you're actually asking me, to be frank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's an answer too. Thank you for that. Now, in this programme, it goes on to state that you advocated a new relationship towards the provinces, that it should be re-examined and assessed in a more modern way.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in the programme, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it also say that the power wielders of the one-party system unilaterally and uncritically imported the concept of provinces from the Soviet constitution to the post-war Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in the programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then does it say later on again through the one-party power wielders, that is to say the Communist Party, the provinces were transformed into states?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the programme says as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it go on to say that such a grotesque project become a destabilising factor of states who have them and it is because of them that human blood is spilled? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's what it says. I remember that from the programme itself but I can't find it in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you, is it true that this was done by the constitution of 1974, which in fact was the found works for the establishment of eight states, two of which were on Serbian territory? De facto was that how it was in practice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The federal functions of that state through the right of veto, were they upset, completely?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this provide the ground works for disintegration and the break-up of Yugoslavia itself, ultimately? Did this provide the grounds for that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to political assessments, and if we look at the state of affairs in practice according to what you said, the republics did have a high degree of competence. Now, I don't know what you mean by whether this constitutes grounds for breaking up Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this right to secession became the dominant right in that particular 1974 constitution, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Let me put it this way: The right to secession was interpreted by individual republics as the right of the republics to secession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking whether that principle became dominant in the constitution. I'm not talking about who wanted to secede when.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't hear you properly. Would you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The right to secession, did that become in a way dominant in the constitution? Did Kardelja who was the creator of the constitution say way back in those days that Slovenia was in Yugoslavia only in a transitory fashion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, these are historical facts. I think that that's what was talked about and stated at the time. I can't guarantee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is this: By that constitution on the territory of Serbia, was the principle of one citizen, one vote made impossible and that the veto of Vojvodina and Kosovo, did it take away the right of the Serb peoples that the other nations enjoyed? The other nations enjoyed this right in their own republics?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how the Serbs interpreted it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. The principle of one citizen, one vote, could it have achieved anything on the territory of Serbia? That is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the principle was realised at the level of the provinces, republics, federation. In this context, it reflected the dissatisfaction and the Serbian Democratic Party shared the view in Serbia that this was not a good thing for Serbia to give the provinces a status of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you write your proclamation because you considered that Kosovo had all autonomous rights but not a right to its own state, a state of its own?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the party line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in Krajina, in the 50 years from 1945 onwards, did you advocate cultural, political, and territorial autonomy for you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in 1956.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as somebody who headed that state at one point in time, as you yourself did, I'm sure you know these basic facts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs advocated through the institutions of the republic and outside the institutions through the Serbian Arts and Cultural Society when was proclaimed from a cultural to a political institution, and it advocated in this way the founding of the Serbian Democratic Party and other parties. I've already spoken at length about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May I go back to a moment to one of the intercepts, a conversation between Dobrica Cosic and Radovan Karadzic, tab 50, 353. And I don't think we need look for it, Your Honours, because what I'm going to read out is something that has already been asked an interpretation by the Prosecutor. Radovan Karadzic says: "Otherwise, they, the people who drew up the map, have drawn up the most honourable and honest variation where we have 61.3 per cent of the area." "Ah 61.3," says Cosic. And Karadzic's response to that is, "Otherwise, according to the historical right, we would have had 70 per cent." Now, I'm not going to ask you to interpret any of these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conversations because I consider that this will be something that Their Honours will do looking at them in their entirety, but what I want to ask you is this. As we're discussing Karadzic's and Cosic's conversation, private property, this is my question to you: Is a private property the unassailable right of each and every individual and a sanctity, private property?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the political programme was advocating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the land registers and excerpts from them proof that the country belongs to somebody and houses on a given property? Is this all contained in the land registry and cadastre? That something that is contained there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Proof of ownership of property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, 70 per cent of the country was privately owned in Bosnia by Serb ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know that for a fact yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you held the position you held, do you know of the 17.200 square kilometres, that is the surface area of Croatia, which portion of the land in Krajina was privately owned by the Serbs, by Serb citizens?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our facts and figures, more than 12 per cent of the land was owned by the Serbs. At least that is one of the figures that appeared, which we accepted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about Croatia. I'm asking you about Krajina, Lika, Kordun, Banija.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know we didn't look into the cadastre and the square areas of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said you didn't know how many inhabitants Krajina had exactly and you couldn't answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Take it slowly, please. What was it I didn't say exactly and specifically yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you didn't know how many inhabitants Krajina had at one particular point in time. You said 500 and something-odd.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, that related to the census and the results of the population centres. The number of citizens that went to vote on Serb autonomy on the 19th of August until the 2nd of September, 1990, and I said in that regard that Serbs in Croatia went to the referendum as well as Serbs who lived in Yugoslavia and in the diaspora in Paris. I think that's what my answer related to. I don't know how you interpreted me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
