utterances.text: Well, although you advocated many rights of persons in those areas, as you yourself say, you were at the head of a state and you proclaimed that state at one point in time, and you don't know, according to the land registry, how much land is owned by Serbs in the area you were the head of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't look into things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back and refer to the programme once again. In response to a question from the Prosecutor, you said that the main obstacle to the establishment of political democratisation was the domination of one party, and that was the Communist Party.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that in the programme?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the programme?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In elementary school -- in secondary school, third grade elementary school I became a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, in December. Well, I was a young person, and in 1990 I was -- I was a member of the Communist Party up to 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you -- is it true that you attended a party congress several months before that? Well, I'm not asking you that actually. Is it true that no opposition bloc broke down the party but that its members disbanded the party itself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't speak about any disbanding or demolishing. I just said how the League of Communists of Yugoslavia at its last congress changed the party statute, and I said that I voted against the change to the statute although it already been imported. What are you actually asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 78, we looked at tab 78 yesterday, I believe, Exhibit 352/2, and this is contained in the documents sent to us by the Prosecutor, you were, shown a law yesterday, a law enacted by you personally as president, you yourself brought about this law on the 9th or 7th of January, 1992, and you signed the act on banning the work and political action of all political parties, organisations, et cetera, on the territory of Serb Krajina. Now, if you brought this decree into effect, you're a member of the party, and just one year after you ceased to be a member of the League of Communists, you banned people -- you did not let people allow the right to rally over one idea and ideology. You banned the existence of these parties. Whereas you yourself had been a member of the party for 20 years, after which you passed a law saying that people were not permitted to rally around an idea, an ideal.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that this took the form of a law but it was a political act to distance ourselves from Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means you banned people from having the right to think for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained the object of that particular document, of that decree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what about all the former members of the League of Communists? Did they all become high ranking officials later on in the newly established states? Did they become the presidents of those states straight away and some of them very high positions? All those who had formerly been members of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, which meant that they stayed in power.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were reformists, joined other parties. Others remained in some functions. Others remained rigid and conservative such as Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Gligorov, Kucan, other cases in point, not to mention the others. Now, as this is related to credibility, answer me this, please: Yesterday in your response to a question about the 169.000-odd dollars, US dollars, you said you didn't remember that sum of money, having received that sum of money.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I don't remember. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you answer me this: Do you not remember the court proceeding -- legal proceedings taken against you? This was not -- could not have been public, but it was done covertly. Secrete legal proceedings were taken against you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the intercepts that had to do with arrests Milan Martic, and we listened to them mostly, everything that took place, according to what we heard only the intercepts was geared towards preventing one incident from taking place; isn't that right? And this was an incident that led to unrest among the population.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerned the release of Martic from detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But without any incident; isn't that right? Were the people to serve? Did they gather?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything was done to release Martic. That was the purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. That was more important than avoiding an incident. Was the incident avoided? Was the incident avoided?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking of the purpose of those talks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One wonders whether you can interpret something on your own. That is something that Their Honours will decide about. But I would like to know, among all those 50 intercepted conversations, did you hear anyone issuing an order to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard Slobodan Milosevic issuing an order to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To gather people to report to Zelac, to organise a rally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is to any military authority. I'm always referring to Krajina itself.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anyone, I'm not mentioning Slobodan Milosevic, I don't know why you're mentioning him. I'm saying whether among those 50 intercepted conversations you heard a single one in which somebody was giving orders to the Supreme Command to do something. Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the form of an order to the Supreme Command? I did not hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'll ask you some notorious facts in my opinion, and upon -- after that, I will have a question for you. It is true -- is it true that on the 2nd of July, 1990, the Assembly of Slovenia adopted a declaration on the sovereignty of the state of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly around that time. I don't remember the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just confirm the fact. Is it true that on the 23rd of December a plebescite was held in Slovenia at which 88 per cent of the population voted in favour of independence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on the 31st of January, the Assembly of Slovenia adopted a charter saying that it would start proceedings for disassociation from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Drnosek [phoen] informs the Presidency about this and, then the 18th of May 1991, the Assembly of Slovenia addressed to Assembly of the SFRY a statement on disassociation from Yugoslavia not later than the 26th of June, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly so, but I don't remember the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Slovenia adopts of the resolution on disassociation from Yugoslavia. And then there's a referendum in the republic and then on the 25th of June, Croatia and Slovenia actually proclaimed their independence.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 30th of June that Croatia did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Were those moves that led to the disintegration Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were laws which made Slovenia and Croatia independent states ready to enter into a confederation with other countries that were willing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that comes later. They proclaimed their independence. Now, whether they associated with others, that's something else that comes much later; Badinter speaks about that. Leave that aside for the moment. Here on page 13011 of the transcript, line 16/21, you said that there was a discussion about future relationships in Yugoslavia and that this was a very intensified discussion regarding two possible options. One, the political approach upheld by Serbia, a strong federation, and a second one by Croatia and Slovenia, independence and secession. You repeated that several times; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If things evolved in this way, that is the proclamation of independence, the adoption of all these legal acts and documents in that connection, was the discussion over that issue over? There were no more discussions as of June?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June, around the beginning of June, upon the intervention of the European Community and the agreement in Brioni, the decisions of Croatia and Slovenia were suspended for three months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. These legal acts adopted by Slovenia and Croatia, didn't that mean that there was no further discussion about it as far as they were concerned? They had a discussion, they implemented their decisions, and there proclaimed their independence, so that there was nothing more to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they insisted on recognition of their independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If that is so and after your interpretation of a conversation between Slobodan Milosevic and Karadzic, this is page 13046, the transcript of the 19th of November, you said, and these were all conversations dating back to July and August, after all these discussions and after what Slovenia and Croatia had done, you said there was a plan for Slovenia and Croatia to be forced to leave Yugoslavia and thereby the disintegration to be carried out. How could they have had such a plan, as you interpreted the conversation, if by then those legal documents had already been adopted? They had made the decision, and somebody saying, "They're shooting at our backs, and what can we do that we can't go on living together under those conditions?"

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure of the proclamation of independence and the leaving of Yugoslavia by Slovenia and Croatia started in January 1991, and it proceeded in a way that we've --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but we've already said that it was completed in June. In June it was all over. And these intercepts were later. All of them were later. Why would somebody be making a plan to force somebody to leave when he's already decided to be independent and he had already left?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was happening in the events that took place prior to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We now have the Exhibit 351, tab 64. Even before them, without any prior procedure, on the 18th of March, 1991, you signed the decision for Knin to secede from Croatia. How big is Knin? How is it possible that you could do this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was made on the basis of the decision of the executive council of SAO Krajina of the 16th of March, 1991, and the decision was prompted after my telephone conversation with Mr. Milosevic when he asked us to support Yugoslavia, and that meant to remain in Yugoslavia in line with his option which meant separating from Croatia and remaining in Yugoslavia and letting Croatia go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already said during your testimony that Slobodan Milosevic didn't know about it and that he even opposed it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said how I interpreted his request to support Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you seceded though he didn't ask you to do that. He didn't oppose secession. But you said explicitly that regarding that, or the decision of the 1st of April, 1991, when the whole of Krajina seceded from Croatia, did not have his support.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That decision was taken after a telephone conversation with Milosevic and his request that we support Yugoslavia. This was a -- that was the way in which we supported Yugoslavia. His option for the Serbs of Croatia to remain in Yugoslavia and for Croatia to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did he oppose that? When he learnt that you had taken such a decision, were there protests because he did that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't oppose the decision on secession. He opposed the decision on unification with Serbia. He said with Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said over the past few days that he did not agree with that, but let it be. From those days, that is in that period up to May 1991, was the JNA normally deployed throughout the territory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let us say until the beginning of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the beginning of 1991? I didn't notice any special or unusual activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that 50-year period up to 1991, did it occupy anyone on the territory of Yugoslavia or was it the regular army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was the armed force of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, something in the -- in this connection? Do you know that on the 27th of June, 1991, the Territorial Defence of Slovenia attacked the JNA without any prior announcement and that 50 soldiers were killed? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the JNA intervened upon the demand of the federal government to deblock frontier posts and that there was an armed clash with Slovenian Territorial Defence forces and fire was opened on unarmed soldiers. I don't have any specific information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this not followed by attacks and occupation of barracks in both Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how the armed conflict occurred between the JNA and the armed forces in Slovenia. As for Croatia, I've already said that the conflict started as of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to read out two documents to you. If I could have that much time, at least. I have much more. Both documents were signed by you. They are your orders. One has been tendered into evidence. It is tab 38, 352/2. And the other has not been admitted into evidence but it is tab 37. Tab 37, 352/2. You are issuing an order on the 1st of April, 1991, and you say as follows: "Order: To carry out mobilisation on the 1st of April." You're saying to mobilise the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina and volunteer units to defend the freedoms of all citizens and to protect its territorial integrity. This is number one. And number two, that is the only thing the Prosecutor read to you: "We demand from the government of the Republic of Serbia to have for the forces of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia to provide all technical and personal aid to the SUP of Krajina." So this was your order and your conclusion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already commented that document here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the conclusion but not the order.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That order too was the result of the events in Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But what was not tendered into evidence, tab 37, on that same day you have a request dated the 1st of April, 1991, and now you're not writing to anyone in Serbia but to the Presidency of SFRY, the JNA command staff, the federal SUP, and other federal organs, competent federal organs, requesting strongly first: "Urgently and entirely to implement the decision of the Presidency of Yugoslavia on the complete withdrawal of aggressor and terrorist forces of MUP of the so-called republic of Croatia from the territory of the SAO Krajina." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That was in connection with the promise of Milosevic and Jovic that JNA would protect the territory of the Serbs in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you put that in your request to Serbia? But you are writing to the Presidency of SFRY here.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's also what you said in your interview with Grubac on the 18th of January. I can't find it now. You said the same thing there in that interview. You also spoke about terrorist and aggressor forces already in January; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Figuratively, that's how we spoke of each other. I spoke about the terminology used between us and the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but under 2 of this request, you knew nothing about the victims of the Serbs or their casualties or anything, but here you said to immediately return the bodies of the dead and all the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was confusing, and there were reports that many people had been killed and disappeared in the area of Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you're writing a request that you signed. Are you doing that on the basis of unverified information or do you have reliable information when you demand the return of the dead?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the information received from the people from Korenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have no direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there, and I was told that it had happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a single body?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One person was killed on the Serbian side and one policeman on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here it says "dead bodies," in the plural. But let's go on. Number 3, request number 3: You're demanding through the mediation of the Red Cross of Yugoslavia and the federal SUP - again the federal - that all detained citizens and members of Krajina SUP -- and how many were detained?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is true. I know that Hadzic was elected -- was arrested in Plitvice at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on page 3064 of the transcript, you go on to say: "The JNA entered into the war with Croatia in August. The conflict started in May." And here, in these orders, you're referring to certain requests of your own for assistance from federal institutions.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the guarantee of Jovic and Milosevic, that they would protect us in connection with those events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, on the 13046, you said there was a plan for a part of Croatia which was occupied by the JNA and which was under the control of the Serbs to remain in Yugoslavia. Are you referring to Krajina when you said that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the truth something else? In those days, the army -- in those days, the army hadn't occupied anything. The army had been occupied itself or, rather, surrounded, under siege. What particular period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most critical period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May, June, July, and August, and September, and October?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke with precision about the escalation and how the JNA was used. I spoke with precision about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here you talked about occupation, and a moment ago we read out that you submitted a request to prevent the activities of terrorist organisations.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When giving my answers, I must know exactly to what time period you're referring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you made this request in April. Was there a war on already?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that already in August 1990, via Jovic, Milosevic said that he would protect our political struggle, and he said the same during all meetings with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I have to hurry up. Did you refuse three times the Carrington Plan? The talks you had with Wijnaendts in the autumn of 1991, each time Milosevic told you to accept and each time you rejected?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three talks with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already said that here.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two were the same in meaning, the third was different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not once did you accept his recommendation. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On two occasions he was forcing us to accept the Carrington Plan and the third time he asked us not to accept it because he said special status on Yugoslav soil, and this was contrary to the Carrington Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm saying that he said to you twice accept the proposals made and you didn't. Did anyone from the parallel structures perhaps force you to accept it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those times, there was a parallel structure. Frenki was waging a campaign against me as a traitor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's not go into that. Did Frenki tell you not to accept the plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki was the parallel structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Frenki tell you not to accept the plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic told us to accept, and I said here in court that I did not agree with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That's what I wanted to hear. What about the Serbian National Council on the 19th of December, 1991? Did it proclaim the Republika Srpska and form a state thereby?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the Serbian National Council but the Assembly of SAO Krajina proclaimed itself to be constitutional and did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Slobodan Milosevic opposed to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear him oppose it. In a telephone conversation with me, he only said -- he called me "colleague" in a sort of mocking way, sarcastic way, and when he called me to attend a meeting on the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, did you insist upon linking up with the rest of the parts, Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, that it should all form one state and sent a request to the international community to ask for it to acquiesce?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened was the following: On the 19th of December, the SAO Krajina was proclaimed the Republic of Serbian Krajina and then Eastern Slavonia and Western Slavonia themselves took the decision to become annexed to the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Vance-Owen Plan? Did Milosevic say that it should be accepted and you refused?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan did not apply to Krajina. It applied to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Vance-Owen Plan did not apply to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what you were discussing, the Vance Plan, did he insist you accept it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milosevic not only insisted but imposed the acceptance of that plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself were against?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was against in the way that I have explained here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. That brings me to the point that I'm interested in most, and perhaps it will interest the Trial Chamber as well; why you failed to agree to the Vance Plan, was that precisely the fact that you did not want to have demilitarisation because you were opposed to the UN -- to the JNA pulling out of the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you insist that the demarcation line be along the borders between Krajina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the UN peacekeepers should come and be deployed along the green line, as it was known.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Tapuskovic. Microphone for the amicus, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone. Your microphone seems to be off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on one occasion Milosevic told you where the army should be deployed, and now I see here that you yourself insisted upon the boundary being between Croatia and Krajina, otherwise you wouldn't give your permission for the plan to be signed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're distorting my words. Milosevic said where the army would be deployed in mid-June -- July 1991, and over the Vance Plan discussions, I demanded that the JNA remain where Milosevic had had it deployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nonetheless, despite the fact that you were asked to agree, was it in the interests of one and all to have the agreement signed and the war ended and the suffering ended? But you prolonged it and did not accept the plan; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are making some assertions. What do you want to say by that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't accept the plan.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't accept the plan for security reasons and I have discussed that in detail here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Assembly of Krajina accept the plan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Krajina Assembly did, after the Security Council decision to send UN peacekeepers to the -- and the Municipal Assembly of Knin, which I presided over, on the 12th and 13th of March, accepted the deployment of the UN peacekeepers on its territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, did you, with the part of the Assembly that did not wish to accept the Vance Plan, did you with that portion of Assembly members, make a decision to hold a referendum?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision to hold a referendum came on the 12th of February, 1992, and the Security Council decided on the 20th and 22nd of February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you wanted to hold a referendum to prevent the adoption of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wanted to hear the people state its views. This was before the UN Security Council had decided to send the peacekeepers into Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if I'll have time for all this. I'll have to skip over some questions, but I'm interested in everything concerning plan Z-4, the Z-4 plan, and it concerns tab 104, Exhibit 352. It is the document of the United Kingdom embassy and its letter. We looked at it. Did you have the document in your hands? It is in English.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was read out to me in the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to that plan, did you hold two conversations with Slobodan Milosevic as you yourself said? Once, I think you said according to the transcript on page 13242, that you talked to him for the first time about the plan in April and that Slobodan Milosevic, as you said, told you that the plan was a good one but that there were just some minor problems with respect to the territory around Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said the plan was good and that Slunj should be vertically divided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And the second time you talked to him was in the night between the 2nd and 3rd of August, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd of August, at about 11.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, about these conversations with him, did you inform Gavro -- Galbraith, did you inform Galbraith of your talks with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discussion with Milosevic on the 3rd was after my talks with Mr. Galbraith. I talked to Mr. Galbraith in the afternoon of the 3rd and he asked me whether I had made a statement. I said that I had. I think that was the contents of my telephone conversation with Galbraith on the 3rd of August in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you didn't tell him what was told you in the month of April by Milosevic, that the plan was a good one. You didn't convey that to Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you quite frankly, Galbraith said that Milosevic was the greatest adversary to the plan, opponent to the plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In point 4 of the document, Galbraith said that you yourself said that Martic and Milosevic were opposed to the plan. You did not tell Galbraith what Milosevic had told you, namely, that the plan was a good one. What it states here is that you said that Martic and Milosevic were opposed but that you had nothing against it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. I did think that Milosevic was not -- was not frank and honest with me in the conversation I had with him in April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you talked to Galbraith in the morning, and you told him that you would make this public. Beforehand, you had spoken to Milosevic and once again you didn't say that Milosevic had said, "Yes, yes, but calmly, peacefully."

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I mentioned Milosevic to him later on over the -- in the telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell anybody from the month of April onwards that Milosevic had said the plan was a good one, which meant that it ought -- it should be accepted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I -- I don't remember that I kept that secret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why didn't you emphasise it when you spoke to Galbraith?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Galbraith that he -- Milosevic must give his agreement, especially with respect to the involvement of forces around the Bihac pocket. That was emphasised in particular. The army was there, the army of the RSK, Abdic's forces, the MUP of Serbia, the DB of Serbia and everybody else that took part, and especially it was around this Bihac pocket that I emphasised to Galbraith that this could not go ahead without Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's see what it says in paragraph 4 of the document. You said to Galbraith that he personally wanted to accept this, and then you say Martic and Milosevic were opposed, full stop. Is that what you said? Is that what you were thinking?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic said that Milosevic was opposed to taking the plan into consideration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. You told Galbraith what is written here, that Milosevic was opposed, although on that night as well you had an answer and his answer was, "Yes, but calmly, peacefully, without any incidents, talk to some man called Rade and then settle the terms." You didn't say that in April you had his support and that he had said that the plan was a good one.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference between what Milosevic said "calmly, peacefully," and I think the interpreters here translated the word "min" or "slowly" properly the first time, which means without panic. It was taken to mean slowly. It did not mean slowly; it meant calmly, peacefully. So there was a difference between what Milosevic stood behind and what he meant when he said "min" or calmly, yes, yes, when he wasn't involved himself. I know the difference of when he is actually standing by what he says and is saying what he means and when he isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether I'll have one or two minutes more. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'll try and pass over some issues quicker, get through some material quicker. I have a list here that I have drawn up, and I should like to hand it over to the Trial Chamber itself to facilitate matters. They are 54 decisions, in fact, and each of these decisions was signed by Babic, and they were all made between July and December 1991, amongst which were two orders for mobilisation and the order where he releases -- places a citizen at liberty without any court decision to do that. And I should like it to be known that between - and I'm drawing your attention, Your Honours, to this - that between July and December 1991, there are 54 decisions by Mr. Babic which relate, among others, to and first and foremost the functioning of the Territorial Defence, and I have made a list of them all. I have them in English as well with the numbers, and I will give you some copies to distribute amongst yourselves. It's difficult for me to find my own way round all this. But we have here a decision. First it is tab 25, 351/1. It is the order dated the 2nd of August, 1991, signed by Milan Babic. And the other decisions are similar to this. He states: "Pursuant to the aforementioned law, the commander of all the armed forces on the territory of defence of Zagreb is the president of the government of Krajina Milan Babic," answer signs it, and then he goes on to state once again an order by him to the commander of the Territorial Defence, the Territorial Defence zone area commanders are appointed by the commander of the Territorial Defence of Krajina i.e., the Prime Minister Milan Babic. I assume that these orders were arrived at by you independently or did somebody exert pressure on you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I made them independently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you parallel structures have nothing to do with this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parallel structures are something quite different I've already explained this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Frenki perhaps order you to do this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we come to another one. 162. That is the order, the same exhibit. The order for mobilisation. And then another order, once again for mobilisation, dated August. Did you issue that order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you read out the order exactly, please, and I'll tell you then?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This one is dated the 26th of October, 1991. The order is in Serbian, but it refers to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the order received from the Yugoslav state Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you issued this yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So I won't go back to that. So all these decisions show that you made your decisions yourself and made all these 54 decisions. You arrived at these decisions at your own initiative; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quote each and every one to me and I'll be happy to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I haven't got time to do that, but all of them were signed by you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you talked to Slobodan Milosevic twice about financial matters. The first time was in 1990 when you discussed the Viga factory. There was no war at that time. There were no armoured trains or bombs or anything of that kind, just screws were being manufactured there, and you asked 60 million, a sum of 60 million to save the factory. Was that the principle of solidarity that held true in Yugoslavia, that when there was a problem, everybody should pull their efforts to help, the principle of solidarity among the republics, did it exist at that time? When a factory had to be saved, did everybody help?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was support of the municipality of Knin to the municipality of Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next conversation you had was in 1993 in a delegation when you talked about financial issues; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this isn't actually a question. What I would like to do is the following: I would like to show the Trial Chamber and draw your attention to the following so that Their Honours could take this into consideration. I won't able to do so when the Prosecution presented its evidence. I couldn't keep getting up with my own remarks and criticism so I'll do that now so Your Honours could take this into account. I think that the Court ought to assess in respect to all the financial documents that relate to the time after 1992, June 1992, in fact, afterwards. So after the incriminated time in the indictment. What has that got to do with the events up until June? You yourselves will be able to assess that. But I should like to draw your attention to the fact that those documents, for the most part, with two exceptions, were documents after June 1992, which means when the conflict that is mentioned in the indictment no longer took place. There are only two documents prior to that time frame, time period. One was the 10th of February, 1992, and it was 380.000 dinars. That was the sum that was in question. And it is 352 document, tab 16. It was the events in Glina and relates to the events in Glina. They were not used. But it emerges from that document that some banking assistance was called for so that the money which was already in Glina could be used in the republic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, for MUP too, but it was a sum of money that was already there, and the sum was 380.000 dinars. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it would appear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second document is document 352, tab 5 and 6, which talks about -- it doesn't talk about the money received but a programme of assistance that is to be received in the future, and the Prosecution has calculated this and found that it is 92 million marks and that these are monies incurred, demands for such-and-such assistance even after June. Before June and after June as well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What documents are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about financial documents in which you ask for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked for assistance, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any proof that 92 million German marks were given to you ever, that the sum of 92 million German marks arrived in Krajina at all?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any document to prove that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no -- do you have any documents that your requests were complied with and that this sum actually reached you, this sum of 92 million German marks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents I had I have supplied you with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And may I conclude and deal with one more topic? You said here, you spoke here and we have it in the transcript on page 13002 and also in tab 352 -- or, rather, Exhibit 352, the tab is 26, where you spoke about the fact that the media in Serbia exaggerated events and that you came under the influence of the media too and that frequently you based your own opinions on what the media was saying. What about the influence of the Zagreb media, the television and press? Did that also have any influence on your own judgement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which had greater weight?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The media from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, all that was being written at the time about changes in the constitution, depriving the Serbs of their rights, all this disturbed you less than the articles appearing in the Serbian press.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way in which the press in Serbia were explaining this. We, and I personally had greater trust in the press in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you devote more attention to what was actually happening in Krajina and Croatia and all over Yugoslavia than to what you read in the papers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To both the events and the press.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But which more?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered with great precision. I can't wait now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that some people brought pressure to bear on you, that you accepted their rhetorics and you thought the same as they did?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I name the people I meant, the rhetorics I referred to and the time period I referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the letter you wrote in response to Milosevic when you rejected the Vance Plan, were they all your positions or Rasuo's positions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were my positions as well. I accepted them. I adopted them as my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you signed what they had written.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I adopted it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you wrote in the letter which Mirko Marjanovic allegedly asked of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said under what circumstances I had done that. I was asked to say that Yugoslavia was not to blame, and this was a condition for the refugees to be admitted in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about what is said in the letter what happened to the people before they reached Serbia? That is not true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I entered in my statement, the part of my statement that was requested by Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what that letter says about the suffering of Serbs on their way to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what is correct? You said what happened once they arrived in Serbia. Allegedly they were sent to Kosovo. But what happened to them while they were travelling to Serbia? What were the casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many were many. People were dying along the way. There was a shortage of water, food. The trip took a long time. There were blockades. Then Mladic put up a blockade at Vrbas. So Mladic is to blame for the blockade on Vrbas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you about what was happening on the motorway when columns of refugees were bombed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the column from Topusko. The column was shelled at Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that several were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question and that will be all. You spoke at length here about many things, but mostly you never saw anything. You just received information.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true. I also said about what I saw. And in most cases, I was an eyewitness of many of the events I saw. I said exactly which events I had seen, which I received reports about, and which I heard about later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever take a decision on the battlefront? Did you take part in any battle? Did you really see what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see things. I spoke about the events in -- around Korenica. I was at Miocic when colonel -- now, what was his name -- Djukic was in command of the artillery firing at Petrovo Polje, and once I was at Peruca, but I didn't see any combat. The units were further forward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever take command yourself personally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you said you had half an hour in re-examination; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It will have to be on Monday morning. Mr. Babic, I'm afraid we must ask you to remain for another weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have two technical points to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it have to do with Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, at least one. One refers actually to a remark that Mr. Milosevic made this morning. He said actually that now the tapes of the suspect interview would be available to the public, and that is actually not the case because only a very, very limited part of the tapes are in evidence. So I just want to make this remark that it -- the entire tapes of the suspect interview with Mr. Babic are not to be disclosed, so that everybody understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have to consider that. It will be a matter for the Trial Chamber, of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And the other point is just the order of the witnesses for next week. We want to actually achieve, to conclude all the witnesses who come from abroad and would put Mr. Blewitt the end of the row and not at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. He is simply producing, as I remember, some documents which another witness -- have -- are they in evidence? They are. Right.

utterances.text: Yes. Well, produce another clip, if you would, when he comes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that you said that you would consider this matter regarding the disclosure of the tapes, would you please bear in mind that even this last statement that he gave in connection with the letter, answering questions by Mr. Tapuskovic, differs significantly from what is on the tapes and the questions I put to him, because on the tapes he is complaining that Rasuo wrote a letter that he did not agree with, and now he's saying that he agreed with it and wrote it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is all -- this is all matter of argument. We will consider how much of the tapes should be admitted. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, if you'd like to think about that and you can address us next week as to which bits should be allowed in and which not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no problem with allowing the entire tapes, which is actually more than 1.000 pages into evidence. I only mentioned that at the moment it's not and that is why I made the remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will consider that. Meanwhile, 9.00 on Monday morning. There is a motion for a protective measures of the 4th of December which the Prosecution have put before us.
